speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
That, notwithstanding any Standing or Special Order or practice of the House, for the purposes of consideration and disposition of Bill C-49, An Act to provide for the resumption of certain government services:
1)	there shall be, following the adoption of this Order, one day for the report stage and one day for the third reading stage of the Bill;
2)	on each of the said days, at 15 minutes before the time normally provided at the conclusion of Government Orders, the Speaker shall interrupt any proceeding then under way and shall put forthwith, successively and without further amendment or debate, every question necessary to dispose of the said stage of the Bill; provided that if any such day be a Monday, Tuesday, Thursday or Friday, Private Members' Business shall commence, and continue for one hour, immediately following such proceedings; and
3)	following such hour of Private Members' Business or, on other days at the conclusion of proceedings on Bill C-49, as the case may be, the Speaker shall adjourn the House.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise, with not a great deal of pleasure to speak to this motion. The intent of the motion before the House is to try to speed up, without in any other way seriously inhibiting the present Standing Orders vis-a-vis Bill C-49.
Bill C-49, as the House will know, is back to work legislation. It is an effort to bring the two groups, that is the Coast Guard workers and the people who work in veterans' homes and hospitals, back to the table in an
Government Orders
effort to settle a dispute between management and workers which has been going on for some time.
I think everyone-except if one lives in a large city in central Ontario such as Ottawa-who has any experience with the weather and the transportation system in this country appreciates the dangers of the oceans at this time of year.
Furthermore I think it is fair to say that the farmers of western Canada who have grain on the ships that are presently in danger of being trapped in the seaway appreciate the great cost to the country that is going to ensue if those ships are trapped in the seaway over the winter. I understand there is a possibility of some 41 ships-which would be a record-that could be caught in the seaway as a result of the actions of the Liberal and NDP parties in stalling this legislation.
That may not bother members from Windsor, but if I were representing Windsor, a seaway port, I would be concerned about it. It does not bother anybody from London, they are landlocked. It does not bother anybody from Ottawa because they do not have emphathy for the people out on ships.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, if they are not concerned about people out on the ships at sea and stalling the seaway over the winter, maybe I could ask the member from Ottawa and the member from Windsor to have some concern for our veterans and the people in veterans' hospitals. These services are presently being looked after by volunteers and if my hon. friend from Ottawa thinks that veterans should be inconvenienced that way and members to have it in their hearts to think about other people.
I see some members here who represent ridings with people at risk on the seas and I do not know how they are going to face their people back home if there are any accidents. I just ask them to think about that. Surely, if I, somebody from Orillia can understand that, the members who have constituents who are at sea might just think about that. They might just think about it the next time they go home.
In any event, I think I have their attention. Kingston is on the seaway. There is the odd big ship going by there but in case of an accident the crews can always swim to shore. That is what these people in Ottawa do not understand.
Why do you not talk to your members from Ottawa and tell them that it may be a big thrill to hold up legislation that puts people back to work if you live in

Government Orders
Ottawa, but if you live somewhere where there is risk at sea, one might have a better appreciation for it.
I did not want to speak for long but I got so incensed at the insensitivity of members opposite that I thought I would put those items on the record. There are some people to which you just cannot get through to.
For fear that there will be some suggestion that we are breaching the rules, I want to point out to the House that there were two ways of moving this legislation through the House; either by a time allocation motion or by this motion. Let us just draw the comparison between a time allocation motion and this motion for fear that after I leave the House there may be some unfortunate comparisons in which there is some variance between the truth and the comments of the members opposite.
One will know that time allocation under Standing Order 78(3) provides for one day at report stage and one day at third reading. This particular motion provides for one day at report stage and one day at third reading. Standing Order 78(3) calls for a two-hour debate. I am sure that by the time we debate this from 11.20 until one o'clock and then probably tomorrow with the opportunity to go until 1 a.m. on Wednesday morning that there will be far more than two hours debate. This will enable us to have met that particular problem in comparison with Section 78(3). The third point that I am sure my hon. friends will want to mention is that they will have the opportunity to speak for longer than 10 minutes. One knows that the debate on a time allocation motion is two hours with 10-minute speeches and the government is providing for much longer speeches by moving.
We think this is an appropriate way to deal with a very serious situation. I would implore my friends opposite to stop the political posturing which may gain some points in Ottawa but which is causing serious problems in other parts of the country where they are just trying to ship grain and look after veterans. I wonder at the reasoning behind the stalling of the opposition parties in not allowing this motion to be voted on immediately and for the report stage of the committee report which was tabled this morning and third reading to go ahead quickly.

Mr. Speaker, first of all, let us remind ourselves, it being Monday morning and the start of another week, what we are doing here. Bill C-49 would provide for the resumption of certain government services.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that this thing started late last week when the government decided to circumvent the normal process of collective bargaining. It used the sledgehammer approach on 3,600 workers, that is 1,300 hospital workers, and 2,300 ships crew people, some of the lowest paid workers in this country. On Thursday and Friday the government began the process of shutting down the collective bargaining process for these people, their right to strike in particular. It arranged to have a committee sitting yesterday, Sunday, in an effort to railroad this whole thing through as quickly as possible. Here we are again today with Bill C-49 and now with a motion to rush things up even more.
Listen, first of all, to the words of our good friend, the government House leader. If piety were for sale, he would be a billionaire. He tells us: "If you lived by the sea"-I say to him, I live by the sea. I will show it to him some time. He might be surprised by how big it is.
It is one thing as a government to try to use its parliamentary majority to bludgeon and hammer people. But on top of that it is an insult to intelligence to say this morning to those 2,300 men and women who earn their livelihoods in very dangerous situations patronizingly: "If you lived by the sea", I say to the minister, that is their first sin. They do live by the sea. The problem is they are not finding enough wages to keep body and soul together by the sea, thanks to this particular stingy government.
Now, the minister tells us as he continues his pious little lecture this morning that he is really helping veterans. I am touched. Where was he when this thing started three and a half weeks ago? Where was the minister's concern for veterans then? He tells us he is concerned about safety. Well, bully for him. If he were so concerned about safety, why was he not talking to the Minister of Transport and the President of the Treasury Board who a few weeks ago were telling us there was no consideration of safety. There was no problem whatever.

When is this honourable crowd going to learn that they cannot have their cake and eat it too? There is either a safety concern or there is not a safety concern, one or the other.
As I review my notes of the pious lecture from the government House leader, I recall that he told us this morning that he and the government are not inhibiting the process. No, no. He probably believes it is midnight outside right now, too. Not inhibiting the process!
For three and a half weeks, it plays with the negotiators on the union side of the table. The government toys with them. Now, day after day, the government brings in every parliamentary manoeuvre it can dream up to shut down the process altogether, trampling on the basic rights of a lot of people. First, the 3,600 people directly involved in this labour dispute. But it went further on Thursday and Friday and particularly this morning. Now it is in the process of trampling on the rights of every parliamentarian in this House because now the government wants to throw the rule book out the window.
Finally, if I may for a moment get away from the particular elements in this dispute, as important as they are, and look in a more global way at this whole issue is about incompetence. This really has to do with incompetence. We would not be here this morning discussing this particular issue if that crowd over there had been competent in their management of the collective bargaining process. That is the problem right there, absolute incompetence.
You only have to go back to late 1987 when Treasury Board missed a deadline for submitting to the Public Service board the list of personnel to be designated essential during the round of bargaining. It missed the deadline. That is basic incompetence, incompetence in the governing of the country, in the administering of the collective bargain agreements and the collective bargaining process. That is where it started, but it did not stop there.
If there is one thing you can say for this crowd, they are consistent about their incompetence. The Tories have used the same tactic here that they used on the free trade issue. When they could not win according to the rules, they threw the rules out of the window. They trampled on the election laws relating to financing of election, and that is another issue we will come back to in time. I just bring that forward now as example to show how this crowd stops at nothing. The law means nothing
Government Orders
to this crowd at all. If you cannot do it within the law, you flout the law.
So the Tories completely missed the deadline back in the fall of 1987 by failing to designate. They could not even do the thing legally and properly. Now they have brought their incompetence one more time to the floor of the House of Commons.
What are the rules we are supposed to live by here, Mr. Speaker? Let me remind you. The rule book we are going by now was written by a committee under the chairmanship of the Hon. James McGrath, now the Lieutenant Governor of Newfoundland. But in that incarnation he was a member of this House and chairman of a committee to rewrite the rules. Before he was chairman of that committee in 1984, he was a member with me and some other people of another committee on reforming the rules. This committee on reforming the rules was chaired by a man who is now a senator, Senator Tom Lefebvre.
In 1982-83, Mr. McGrath, the Deputy Prime Minister, several others in this House and I, 18 of us altogether, did a very thorough review of the rule book, the so-called Standing Orders of this House. Some of the rules were implemented and then, of course, came the election of 1984, and a change of government. So it was appropriate, notwithstanding the fact that Senator Lefebvre had done a magnificent job, that the Tories appoint a government member as chairman of that committee. The succeeding committee was in effect the same committee by another name.
Many of the reforms that were contemplated and designed in 1982, 1983 and 1984 were then refined and recommended to the House, again post-1984, by the then member for St. John's East, Mr. McGrath.
Those rules were embraced to the credit of the Prime Minister and his majority in 1984-85. Those rules, recommended by Mr. McGrath, concocted, designed and crafted by two committees between 1982 and 1985, are the rules that we are using in this Chamber today to the credit of the Prime Minister.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, these rules in theory if allowed to work are a set of rules that makes for a pretty full debate and the representation of the concerns and interests of people from coast to coast. House of Commons rules or Standing Orders, as we call them, like everything else finally depend on goodwill, but particu-

Government Orders
larly do they depend and rely on the goodwill of the majority.
This morning, as you heard from the government House leader, goodwill goes out the window too when this crowd gets its back against the wall. So the government that bungled through incompetence its undertaking, its obligation to give notice of a list of essential service people back in October 1987, now brings its bungling here to the floor of the House of Commons.
I took a minute just now to outline to you the background of the rules under which we live and work here in this Chamber because it reinforces, does it not, the hypocrisy of the government House leader in coming here and saying that we want to suspend those rules one more time. We not only want to hoist or hijack the rules, we now want to accelerate the hijack. We want to speed her up now. We want to ram her through just as fast as we can.
What is the rush? I will tell you what the rush is. I was in Burgeo in my riding two weeks ago and the eight Coast Guard people who work in that community came to me with a letter signed by all eight of them, a letter reasonably worded asking the government to get on with the job of finding a workable, mutually satisfactory collective agreement for those coast guard people. In simple terms, negotiate.
That was the rush and that rush has been on for three and a half weeks. It was on for many months before that, before the people got to the point where they had to use the ultimate weapon in the collective bargaining process, to withdraw their services, to engage in a legal strike. Let there be no doubt about it. It has been a legal strike in every sense of the term.
The government House leader unwittingly this morning gives away the government's game. He talks about the Seaway. For those of you who do not know it, the Seaway is not off the coast near Burgeo. It is not anywhere off the coast of Newfoundland. Indeed, it is not even near Dartmouth where so many of the people are suffering because of this particular strike. That was their sin, that the Seaway did not go by their front doors.
Until such time as there was a bottleneck, an ice jam, a problem, a loss of money for the Seaway and until such time as big bucks were on the line, we heard no talk of safety. We saw ministers stand in this House and deny there was any safety consideration.
The minister this morning, in making his plea to the House, his pious little lecture to the House, his hypocritical nonsense to the House, says that there are some problems in the Seaway that are as a result of Liberal and NDP actions. These were his words. How warped! How warped can you be and still be loose? Because of Liberal and NDP actions, the government House leader says, we've got some problems in the Seaway.
I will tell him why we have problems in the Seaway. It is his incompetence, his stubbornness on this issue not to have settled this thing before it came to a strike three and a half weeks ago. That is why we have problems in the Seaway. If he thinks that is Liberal and NDP action, he should have a talk to himself in the mirror.
Who are you talking to? There's no one over there.

The NDP are back. Have you noticed? They are back this morning.
My friend from Churchill asked me who I am talking to. Let me tell him, because like his colleague in the committee yesterday, this whole issue is obviously passing him by. I will tell him who I am talking to. I am talking to the 3,600 people out there. I am talking to the 1,300 people out there who are on a picket line who would rather be in a hospital doing their thing.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to debate and speak against this motion which the government has introduced. I think it is interesting that in the process that has been involved in these negotiations and in this legislation the government is not only the employer but is using its power, through the legislation, to achieve what it could not achieve at the bargaining table.
This is triply repugnant because it goes against a ruling of the International Labour Organization which found this government in contempt of the convention that is signed by Canada with regard to free collective bargaining.
Let me make reference to that ruling. It is with regard to the 1987 Postal Services Continuation Act, introduced by the government of that time. It is important to realize that that legislation is basically the same as the legislation we have in front of us at this time. In other words, with the legislation forced through Parliament by the government in 1987 which was found in violation of Article 3 of Convention No. 87, the government learned nothing.
Let me read from the finding of the committee. I will not read it all because I only have 20 minutes to cover the whole topic. The committee said that under the circumstances, the legislation was "not in conformity with the principles of freedom of association".
The committee draws to the Government's attention that section 11(1) of the Postal Services Continuation Act, 1987, constituted an interference in the free functioning of union organizations, and violated the right freely to elect representatives, guaranteed to the workers by Article 3 of Convention No. 87.
The committee invites the Government to keep all these considerations in mind in the future.
That was what the International Labour Organization, of which Canada is part, on which Canada has served very well over a number of years, said about legislation passed by this House in 1987. Why would this same government come back two years later and introduce legislation which has already been found in violation of an international treaty? Remember that Canada freely signed the convention, freely signed the International Labour Organization convention. It is expected that when our nation puts its signature to a convention, we should live up to that convention. We did not and the government has obviously not learned a lesson. It is going to continue to violate the International Labour Organization.
I should point out to those members of the government and others who may not understand that this is not an organization just of unions, the International Labour Organization is composed of unions, all the governments of the countries affected, including Canada, and the employers associations. We were not found in violation strictly by a group of unions. We were found in violation by nations throughout the world, by employers throughout the world, and by unions throughout the world. We had a fair tribunal, we were found guilty and here the

government comes back again with essentially the same legislation.
The motion in front of us today will restrict debate on report stage to basically Wednesday afternoon. In other words, after quickly rushing this legislation through committee on a Sunday afternoon, where there was not really opportunity to do any clause-by-clause study, where amendments were really not presented, this House is going to have to go through the amendments which were proposed and were presented to the government ahead of time and deal with them in approximately two and a half hours on a Wednesday afternoon. That is assuming there are no procedural wrangles or the government does not have some other trick up its sleeve to even further limit debate at that time. Two and a half hours to consider amendments at report stage.
As the former labour critic of our caucus, I know that there have been amendments made on back to work legislation in the past. I know that at the present time there are discussions going on to see if this bill can be improved. However, all desire by the government to improve the legislation is taken away if this motion passes. The government members know they can get the legislation through report stage in two and a half hours on a Wednesday afternoon and then they can all go off to their Christmas party.
I think that is one of the reasons for the legislation. Why is it that they are quite willing to speak all night on Tuesday on procedural wrangles, but when it comes to the legislation itself we must have those bells ringing by a quarter to six and we must start voting at six o'clock, just because the Conservatives want to go off to their Christmas party. That is their idea of essential services.
I said that this is an abuse of Parliament. We have in the past, and there are members on the government side who know this, amended back to work legislation. I have said that already. But restricting our debate to two and one-half hours on a Wednesday afternoon takes away any initiative by the government to be reasonable in improving this legislation.
That is especially important to understand because the government is the employer. The employer has written this legislation. It is obviously a concern, not only of the workers but of anybody who believes in fairness, that the employer should write the legislation and then force it through the House, force it through committee, force it through report stage and force it through a quick final
Government Orders
reading without anyone having the ability to effectively amend that legislation.
When the railway workers were ordered back to work the legislation was amended. When the postal workers were sent back to work there were improvements made. This time the government is tiying to thwart that possibility. If you are someone who is being ordered back to work, if you are someone who is losing your union privileges, if you are someone who is going to be subjected to severe fines as a result of this legislation, you cannot feel that you have been treated fairly when the government uses its majority and uses a jackboot approach to the rules of this House to prevent adequate study at each and every stage of this legislation.
The government has said that this legislation must pass because it affects essential services. The government failed, we all know it failed, to designate those employees it deemed to be essential within the time limits required by its own legislation.
If the government thought that these services were essential, why did it not live up to the requirements of its own legislation? Why did it not designate those employees doing essential services as is required by law? My colleague, another former labour critic, says the government is incompetent. That is true. But why, as a result of its own incompetence, would it try to rush the legislation through this House negating all sense of fairness, all sense of decorum, all sense of the rules and procedures of this House and against an international labour organization ruling?
The government House leader got up and said: "Aren't you concerned about safety?". Of course we are concerned about safety. "Aren't you concerned about the veterans?". Of course we are concerned about the veterans, but let me speak on a personal level for a few minutes. Both of my parents worked in the Deer Lodge Hospital which was a veterans' hospital. I visited that hospital a number of times when I was growing up and I saw the plight of the veterans, but I also saw the way the workers were treated by the government. There were low wages in the 1960s and there are low wages today.
If the government is so concerned about the plight of veterans and the way they are treated, then why does it pay the people who work in those hospitals and veterans' homes such low salaries? Why has the government failed, in every way, shape and form, to pay salaries that are equal to those paid to people who work in hospitals run by the provinces or by the municipalities? Why has

A human rights tribunal has already ruled that the government has failed to meet the requirements of pay equity and the government has dragged its heels on that issue. If we allow this government to introduce this motion and pass it through the House without making any attempts to amend the legislation, then this House is being unfair to the employees of the Government of Canada. It is always offensive when one side, in this case obviously the employer, writes the legislation ordering people back to work. It is unfair when the fines in the legislation are so high. It is unfair that people lose their rights as a result of this legislation.
It is unfair for us in Parliament to speed this legislation through because the government finds it inconvenient to do otherwise as Christmas approaches, because the government members want to go to a Christmas party on Wednesday evening, because the government itself failed to live up to its obligations with regard to designating essential employees and because the government really has no understanding of or support for the concept of pay equity or regional development and regional equality. How can we, as parliamentarians, allow them to do this?
Unless there are amendments to this legislation making it fairer, we have no choice but to oppose it vigorously at all stages.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to oppose this motion which is another method of limiting debate on what, as some members opposite have stated here this morning, is a very, very serious issue. A very serious issue it is. This back to work legislation
introduced last week will undermine Canadian values and traditions.
We are dealing with an issue that would allow the government to destroy the collective bargaining process. Ironically, it is this government's own ineptitude which resulted in the situation at hand. I am referring to Bill C-49, an act to provide for the resumption of certain government services. Nicely worded so that Canadians do not read between the lines. They will not be certain just what has been accomplished by this legislation.
Let us be clear about just what is going on. The ships' crews group and hospital services group will be forced to abandon their legal strikes. Both groups have attempted to bargain in good faith with the government since the expiration of their collective agreements. Both groups have merely asked for the right to earn a living, which is hardly an excessive demand. Treasury Board has not attempted to resolve these issues in any way, shape or form. It has done nothing more than use stonewalling tactics from the very beginning.
The introduction of this legislation is basically unjust. There is no need for this legislation and the government should not interfere in any way with the free collective bargaining process. This process has been established in Canada for many years. Inherent in the collective bargaining process is the right to strike although, as we who have been in the collective bargaining business for some years all know, not many people want to strike here or anywhere else.
These unions are exercising their right to strike only to have the government react with strong arm techniques. Not only is this a demonstration of a lack of concern and of caring on the part of government, it also provides us with yet another example of the government's incompetence. The list of illogical and incompetent actions taken by this government continues to grow. I need not give examples because it would take far longer to cite them than the time allotted to me today to speak.
When the collective agreement for the ships' crews group expired in December 1987 the union served notice to Treasury Board. Treasury Board had 20 days after the expiration of the agreement to serve notice designating the group. It let the period expire without designating any of the services as essential. When it later tried to designate the group the Public Service Alliance appealed this move to the Federal Court and won, and rightly so. The Public Service Staff Relations Board supported the position of the Alliance so Treasury Board appealed to



the Federal Court and the original decision was upheld. This went on until September of this year and because of this the collective bargaining process was continually delayed.
If Treasury Board had done the job properly the unions would not have been in a position to strike. It did not and now the government has tabled this legislation and passed it on to a committee, which legislation is intended to force these people back to work.
The scenario I have just described reeks of incompetence on the part of this government. When one asks the government why it is introducing back to work legislation, the answer now is "for safety reasons". As has been stated in this House many times in the last two or three days, safety is not an issue here, as was witnessed this past weekend.
Both groups have been conducting reasonable strikes. In the case of the ships' crews, emergency search and rescue vessels have been on standby across the country and the crews have responded on numerous occasions to life-threatening and disastrous situations. While the workers have exercised their legal right to strike, they have continued to provide emergency search and rescue services to all Canadians.
The same can be said for the hospital service workers presently on strike. The Public Service Alliance has offered to provide essential services but the government contends that the level of services offered are inadequate.
A recent article in a local newspaper suggests that the residents of veterans' homes support the position of hospital workers. One resident is reported as saying, and I quote: "We have very few residents who show resentment. We support the strikers because they are really extraordinary people who have given us the best of treatment".
Where are the serious violations of safety that this government is suggesting? In the case of the hospital workers Armed Forces personnel are filling the gap and at the homes temporary nursing assistants and volunteers are providing services. These hospital workers make between $18,000 and $22,000 per year. That is not very much money to survive on in this day and age. These
Government Orders
workers did not seek out a strike but they were given no choice. In the words of PSAC Vice-President Jim MacE-wen, and I quote: "We didn't seek this strike, but we have an employer who stonewalled us during two years of negotiations, has refused to comply with the findings of the Canadian Human Rights Commission with respect to pay equity. They have so exasperated the patience and goodwill of our members that they see no alternative but to take this type of action".
The reference to the Human Rights Commission decision on pay equity refers to a decision to award those workers $28 million in pay equity settlements. This means that the 1,200 hospital workers are owed $3,000 each. This decision was handed down in July 1987. Twenty months later they were still waiting for their money. Three thousand dollars is a lot of money to these workers. It is the difference between having food on the table or not.
Federal hospital service workers did not go on strike until November 29. A week later the government refused to allow it. The government fails to realize that these workers are undervalued and underpaid. The Human Rights Commission tribunal has called upon the government to compensate these workers for past discrimination, to re-evaluate all positions and to revise the hospital services classification standard to parallel the government services group.
The ships' crews workers legally went on strike on November 13. The major issues, as have been talked about here daily, are wages, hours of work, a sea duty allowance and wage parity between east and west coast workers. Last week in this House I called upon the minister responsible to finalize the wage parity issue and to negotiate the remaining issues. I have been informed that a carrot was dangled before the union, that being drop the other issues and you will get wage parity. The minister denied that such a condition exists. Either he is mistaken or he has been misinformed by his own people because Treasury Board officials have stated that that conditional offer was put on the table.
Last week I also indicated that this strike, in my opinion, could be settled quickly, and it must be. The Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence Seaway economy alone is losing over $2 million a day and there is only

between $5 million and $6 million in dispute between adequate services, but the hospital service workers Treasury Board and the union.	deserve to earn an adequate living.
The minister keeps saying that he is willing to negotiate, and negotiate they did. I say to him, stop talking about it and do it. We can end this strike today.
Maybe that is the real reason behind this legislation. Perhaps this is the minister's idea of negotiating. The true motivation has not been to send the workers back because of safety reasons, but to force them back and to break the unions, thereby setting into motion the gradual elimination of the collective bargaining process in Canada, period.
Once again I must remind the House that these groups are in a legal position to strike. It is their right. Now, through this proposed legislation before us, the government intends to fine these underpaid-and I stress underpaid-workers. The fines are quite large-$500 to $1,000 a day for a worker, $10,000 to $50,000 a day for an individual who is a representative of the bargaining agent, and $50,000 to $100,000 a day for the bargaining agent. Those are awfully high penalties for people making in the vicinity of $20,000 a year.
Let us look briefly at what else the legislation does. It orders all ships crews and hospital service workers back to work immediately. It sets in place binding conciliation, that is, both sides have to accept an imposed settlement. The legislation names two chairpersons to the two boards. Normally the process is for each party to name its members for the board and then the members agree to a chairperson. I say that there is no need to do this at all-just settle the strike.
The government must admit that it has bungled the entire process. But why does the government not lick its wounds, return to the table to settle this mess?
I am acutely aware that there are problems out there and that businesses are being affected by the strike. I have received two faxes over the weekend from businesses in the Great Lakes area. I talked to people in Prince Edward Island. There are problems with the shipment of potatoes. The ships are going to be stuck in the harbours. I can appreciate the problems these people are having, because they have to earn a living. The whole economy of the country is suffering. The residents of veterans' hospitals and homes deserve to receive full and
In order to restore rights to everyone concerned I call upon this government to do the right thing. Negotiate today in good faith. Do not force these men and women to accept an unfair settlement.
The government gave no indication, back when it was negotiating, that it was going to introduce legislation, because it has refused to act in good faith. Sadly, that is typical of everything that this government has done in the past five years.
We must remember that these legal strikes have in no way affected the lives or the safety of the Canadian people. The government is trying to destroy the very existence of collective bargaining in this country, and that is the bottom line.
Because of this I oppose this legislation. We on this side of the House implore the government to settle the strikes fairly and equitably. The government has no right to force these Canadians back to work. That tactic may, more than anything else, affect the quality of service that these groups provide. When you take away a person's legal right to self-expression, you deny them their self-worth and self-dignity. That, Mr. Speaker, will benefit no one.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is worth while right at the beginning to remind the government and members of the House that the day closure was first introduced on this piece of legislation was the forty-first anniversary of the Declaration of Human Rights. There were, I thought, rather eloquent speeches on behalf of all three parties concerning this memorable occasion. But, at the same time, we have to be very aware of how fragile human rights are.
It is not sufficient to simply stand up in the House and acknowledge the forty-first anniversary of this, to say how wonderful the United Nations is and how wonderful human rights are unless we put some kind of action behind those words. Mr. Speaker, I would suggest to you that the action of the government in bringing in closure the first time in this particular round of the debate on this proposed legislation really does show its commitment, or lack thereof, to the whole concept of human rights. That is further exemplified as we go through the history of the dispute between the government, the employer, and some of its employees. These are em-

ployees who, I would point out, are among the most poorly paid in the Canadian civil service.
The government's commitment to human rights and equality are stated on a lot of different occasions. In some cases it has been forced to live up to what ought to be its commitment. Here is an example of where that is the case.
There was a complaint by the Public Service employees in 1981 which actually precedes the life of this government and goes into the life of a previous government. This was a complaint brought by Canadian civil servants against the government wherein one of the groups which we are involved with in this legislation pointed out that they were improperly paid in relation to other groups of civil servants, that is, paid less. The Canadian Human Rights Tribunal decided that that was so. I quote the tribunal's decision, "The parties are agreed that the hospital services (HS group)," which is one of the groups we are dealing with in this legislation, "is predominately female and has received less wages than the general services group, a predominately a male group performing the same work of at least equal value."
The government has fought that decision all through the piece, rather than doing the proper thing. I think it is fair to point out that this decision predates the present government, but that does not excuse it for not having taken immediate action when it did come to power.
Nonetheless, during election campaigns the Prime Minister himself has reiterated time and time again-I am not going to read what he said during election campaigns-that this government is unequivocally committed to affirmative action. He said that it is unequivocally committed to making sure that women receive equal pay for work of equal value. In fact he stated on more than one occasion that there was money actually being set aside in order to accommodate the equalization of pay for work of equal value.
This concept on the part of the Prime Minister goes back as far as the 1984 election when I think the nation as a whole was really quite taken up with what appeared to be the sincerity of that man when he spoke to the
Government Orders
National Action Committee on the Status of Women and other groups during the debates in that election campaign. Subsequently, very little has happened. The fact that the hospital services group in this particular instance did not receive the kind of amelioration for the problem which they faced is evidence that that did not occur. Not only did it not occur between 1984 and 1988, nothing of any particular substance has occurred since the 1988 election.
When we compare the forty-first anniversary of the Declaration of Human Rights and the government's apparent commitment to it and its actions, we can only conclude that there certainly is a sense that the government has not lived up to its commitments. Of course that is really not too surprising considering some of its other actions since it came to power even as far back as 1984.
The problems did not start there. When we look at the problems that the ships crews are having, as well as the problems the hospital groups are having, and compare that to the time when there was another strike in progress a month or two ago with the parole officers and another group of employees in the federal government, we see that these three groups make up the total of those who have gone on strike in the civil service within the last short period of time.
I do not suppose it would be a surprise to anyone if I were to point out that if the government had had its way and followed its usual course of action, then these three groups of people literally would not have been able to strike. Since the inception of the ability of the Public service to go on strike these three groups of employees, along with many others, have not been able to go on strike. That is because each year as contract time comes up, the government designates a certain number of people within particular groups whom it considers to be performing essential services, therefore precluding them from being able to go on strike. This year, that did not occur.
The course of action on which the government proceeded as a result of its having overlooked designating

Government Orders
these people as essential certainly reflects incompetence. It goes back again to its lack of commitment to the very basic human rights which were spoken of so eloquently when this legislation was first introduced. Once the government realized it had made a mistake, once it realized there was a possibility that not only these three groups, but many, many others within the civil service action that it conceived possible to prevent these people from going on strike anyway. Specifically, it went to the courts. It made a mistake, and then went to the courts to try to get the courts to overturn the fact that it had made a mistake. It went to the courts to try and get the decision that these people would be able to go on strike overturned. It went to the courts not once but twice.
I suspect it would have gone to the Supreme Court as well had it not been for the fact that by the time the Supreme Court decision would have been rendered the contract would have long since expired. The government had other fish to fry, other ways of getting these people back to work, even though there was a possibility they may go on strike.
I think it is important to point out, as I said before, that many, many more people within the Public Service were able to go on strike other than those in these three groups. In spite of the fact that many other civil servants had the right to go on strike, because of the government's mistake only those three groups did go on strike. I refer to the parole officers, ships crews and the hospital services people who did go on strike, exercising their democratic right for the first time since 1967, when it first became possible for civil servants to be unionized at all, and ostensibly at least to have the right to strike.
There are some very good reasons for these people to go on strike when for the first time they had the opportunity to do so. It in no way signifies that they are strike-happy. What it does signify is that they had no other alternative. Through all the preceding years of their employment with the government they had been prevented from going on strike. As I pointed out before, they had become the most poorly paid within the civil service. I was on the picket line the other day with them and there were different ones pointing out to me the problems they were having. One woman was a single parent with two children earning $16,000 a year.
I do not think there is a community within Canada where $16,000 with one child constitutes anything above the poverty level. That is an atrociously low amount of money for a person to make who is trying to support a family in any kind of meaningful style.
Another woman, a widow with four children, pointed out to me that she was earning $20,000 a year. I guarantee that at those levels of earning, unless one lives in a rural area that is certainly below the poverty level.
It is shameful that the Canadian government, and I am sure that the Canadian people, would find it impossible to support a situation where the Canadian public are condoning-and I guess that is the only way to describe it-employees of the government making so little money and living in such dire straits.
We have a situation where out of desperation these three groups did exercise their democratic rights. They have gone on strike in order to try, as is the common practice in such a situation, to improve their condition in life.
The arguments put forth by the government concerning the need for this back to work legislation certainly begs a question. We have been through one day of debate. We have been through the legislative committee process on this issue. Nowhere has the government been able to point out that there is any threat to the livelihoods of Canadians, or any threats to the lives of Canadians. There was reference made earlier to a decision of the International Labour Organization. I do not intend to go into a description of how the ILO is constituted, that has already been very well pointed out.
The decision of the committee of the ILO states in part, "Nevertheless, unfortunate as these consequences are, they cannot justify an abridgement of the fundamental rights guaranteed by conventions number 87 and 98, unless they reach the point where they affect the life, personal safety or health of the whole or part of the population." In no case has this been evidenced. The Coast Guard workers, the ships crews group, as admitted to by the government, have exemplified the greatest of responsibility in this situation. Before they went on strike they offered to supply personnel wherever it was necessary in order to protect the safety of the Canadian public on our national waterways. The government admits that in no way has there been any threat whatsoever as a result of the strike.
December 11, 1989

In the case of the hospital group, the hospital services group offered to supply services in their places of work. They offered to provide 8 per cent of the people who would ordinarily do the work. The government said that was not satisfactory. It summarily dismissed the whole situation as if there were no other alternatives which may not have been any more complicated than asking the hospital services group, the Public Service Alliance of Canada, whether or not the 8 per cent was the absolute maximum which they would supply. That was never done. There was a great deal of evidence in the public domain to show that the government was very insincere in its approach to the hospital services workers. In addition, it has been adamant in trying to prevent them from going on strike at all, in spite of the fact that it has been so demonstrably uncaring with regard to its obligations under the decision of the Human Rights Commission.
There have been references made to the different people affected by this strike. There is a veterans home in Saskatoon. Long before these people were able to go on strike legally, the government had taken action to remove people from the home and to put them into different medical facilities within the city of Saskatoon. That was much to the dismay, I would point out, of the families of the people involved. These hospital services workers are a part of the families of these veterans who are in our home. In many cases they are the only families that some of these veterans have, since their own families live very far away. They have become part of the daily lives of these people. Even where the family members do not live great distances away the families themselves have said, "Please do not move these people". It is going to be far more disturbing to them to have them moved. The government could have found a way to accommodate the union's offer to provide the essential services that these people would have required without having disturbed them unduly.
The issue of pay equity with the hospital services workers are something which the government is going to have to address sooner or later. The decree is there. If the government wants to settle this strike quickly, then it can start by showing good intentions by simply saying "Look, we do not have to wait for the long process of the Human Rights Commission Tribunal to be implem-
Govemment Orders
ented." It could just go ahead and do it as it is. I cannot understand why the government has not done that.
These people will never get another chance to strike. If the government is going to designate workers as being essential then I challenge it to pay them as they are as valuable and as essential to society as the government now claims. That has not been the case in the past. If the government is going to designate them, then pay them.

Mr. Speaker, I have some comments about the speech that was just given by my colleague from Saskatoon. The comments that he made deal with a very important principle in this country. It is a principle of paying people what they are worth. It is a principle that this government has absolutely steadfastly refused to adhere to.
We heard a lot of rhetoric in this House over the last number of weeks as this issue came before us. I think my hon. colleague would agree that there are a lot of individuals out there who are not exactly sure what the main issues are that have precipitated the strike and this veiy unusual motion, which I think has only been introduced twice before in this place. Basically, it is an advance closure motion. Not only will this government not negotiate in good faith with the unions and adhere to the collective bargaining principles, it is trying to override the established principles and the standing orders of this place by using strange motions in the House.
What I want to get to is the issue of pay. I think many Canadians out there are saying, "Well, we have these two groups of public servants who are on strike and causing some dislocation in the economy". It is in the economy that the dislocation is taking place-the St. Lawrence Seaway economy. We have heard everybody from all sides of this House say that they are concerned about that, and we are concerned about it.
But let us not blame those employees who have exercised their right to strike for just pay for the work that they do. The individuals that I have talked to who work with the ships crews get paid on average about $20,000 a year-a wonderful salary. People who work in the retail sector, restaurant sector, transportation sector and private sector in the marine industries get paid much more than that. But for some reason this government is hell bent on painting these employees as somehow trying

December 11, 1989
to gouge the public purse, somehow trying to pick the pockets of the taxpayers because of their greed.
I just want to put that on the record. I think my hon. friend will agree, since he has been following this issue as intently as members from my party have been doing. These individuals are getting $20,000 a year. What do they do? They come and say to the government, "We want a couple of things. First of all, we want to negotiate in good faith". They did that for over two years. They did not go on strike the first day that they could have, they negotiated for two years. Did they ask for a 50 per cent increase? No. Perhaps they should have. If they had known they were going to get the treatment that they are getting now in this place by this government, they should have asked for 100 per cent. They would be well worth 100 per cent. But that is not what they did. They came in with a reasonable request.
First, they said, "Don't discriminate against us for the job that we do based on where we live. Get rid of that regional rate of pay". That is exactly what the union asked on behalf of its membership.
The second thing that they asked was that they get paid a shift differential, that they get paid for sea duty. It works out to $177 per month. They asked for a couple of other very small fringe benefits. The over-all cost of the package was not the 17 per cent that the government and the President of the Treasury Board continue to push out, the actual increase was closer to 6 per cent. That is terribly misleading to the Canadian public and a great disservice to those men and women who work as ships crews.
I would like to ask my hon. colleague to make some comment on the government's misleading figures, about this terrible group of ships crews who are looking for 17 per cent, when in actual fact we both know that it is 6 per cent. I would like him to comment on that.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. colleague for the questions. I would point out that that is not the only area in which misleading statements have been made by the government.
There is one very misleading statement that came out as a result of questions in the House of Commons the other day when the President of the Treasury Board implied that the President of the Professional Institute
of the Public Service of Canada was condoning the introduction of back to work legislation.
I have a letter which I am not going to quote, but I would certainly like to put on the record that Iris Craig, president of that organization, wrote to the President of the Treasury Board and stated in no uncertain terms that she was in no way in favour of the back to work legislation and was condemnatory of the government's actions, as the rest of us are.
On the matter of rates of pay, it is very hard to understand why the government would distort what is actually happening. It is true that if these agreements are implemented, the rates will be a little bit higher than the general percentage of settlement within the rest of the public service. But it is not the rest of the public service that is complaining about this, it is the government itself. The basic principle is that this kind of settlement has to be put in place in order for these people to receive the kind of pay that they ought to get.
It is certainly not 14 per cent every year of the contract. For the government to imply that that is the case is so erroneous as to be beyond description. It is a reasonable 5 per cent, 4.8 and 4.6, something like that, over what will probably be, in the end, 42 months. That is certainly what is being negotiated now. I thank my colleague for raising that and the opportunity to respond to it.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to say a few words about the sailors lost at sea in Atlantic Canada the last few days, some of whom were Nova Scotia fishermen.

We all know how cold a Canadian winter can be, but just imagine how cold it is on the deck of a 50-foot fishing boat in seas with 30-foot waves in the middle of December. Imagine trying to work your hands on frozen lines and nets while being sprayed with freezing water. Imagine seeing a huge wave coming at your boat and wondering if the boat can take it.
It appears now that three such vessels were victims of such waves and did not make it.
Any time a small vessel goes to sea there is always a chance that it may not come back. It is still a shock and a great loss when it does happen.
All Nova Scotians feel the loss of these sailors and our sympathy goes out to all those who lost relatives, loved ones and friends in these three related tragedies.

Mr. Speaker, I have previously stood in this House and condemned the government's decisions with respect to the centres of excellence project, in so far as they excluded completely and totally any project from the social sciences or the humanities.
I would like to quote briefly from the words of Allan Bromley, the American assistant to the President for science and technology policy. It is a veiy important quote which states:
Many of the outstanding problems we face today-such as the fate of the environment, the danger of nuclear war, the curse of world hunger, and the burgeoning costs of medical care, to name just a few-are often laid at the door of science and technology. Yet in all of these cases, the science and technology needed to solve these problems are effectively in hand. What we do not know are the social, behavioural, and economic consequences of the various possible courses of action available to us.
On this day, the third symposium of scientists and parliamentarians, I think it is befitting for the government to review its decision and to fund a social science or humanities project.

Mr. Speaker, with all that is happening in the world it is easy to overlook the crisis in Cambodia. Yet immediate international attention is required because of the possible return to power of the reprehensible Khmer Rouge.
Since the Vietnamese withdrawal from Cambodia, the Khmer Rouge have launched a number of attacks and made some territorial gains. Their membership in the opposition coalition, recognized by the UN-thanks ironically to western support-creates a real possibility that they will be participants in a future Cambodian government.
I urge the Prime Minister to withdraw Canadian diplomatic support for the coalition and to oppose any new arrangement which would include the Khmer Rouge. Canada must also pressure other nations to follow suit and to act together to have China exercise a more responsible role in that region.
It is also time-indeed overdue-that Canada put in place, through non-governmental organizations, a development assistance package for Cambodia. Improved ties with the Hun Sen government might also be in order.
Finally, let us look at improving ties with the Vietnamese government. The war in Vietnam is long over. Vietnamese troops have now left Cambodia. Let us try to reintegrate Vietnam into the international community.

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon our country paid a last tribute to the victims of the tragic incident that occured last Wednesday. As a result of these events, we have given serious thought to some of the situations in our society.
Today, I would like to consider one of these situations in particular, namely, child abuse.
In some countries, children die of hunger. They cannot ask for help because they do not have the strength to do so. In our supposedly wealthy and civilized country, there are also children who cry for help. These children have been abused, shifted from foster home to foster home, and often left fo fend for themselves.

December 11, 1989
There are children who are unloved, street children, children of divorced parents, unwanted children. And they are all very much alone.
At a time when people talk about the rights of the unborn, and so they should, perhaps we should also consider the rights of those who have already received the gift of life, but a life that is often one of undeserved suffering, with terrifying consequences.

Mr. Speaker, in this last week the Ontario government has committed almost half a billion dollars toward improving the highways in northern Ontario.
Premier David Peterson, the Minister of Transport, Bill Wrye, and the Minister of Northern Affairs, Rene Fontaine, realize the needs of the north. They have acted, and they should be congratulated.
We need this government to develop a national transportation policy which addresses the needs of the highways in northern Ontario.
If the planned cuts to VIA Rail proceed on January 15, residents of rural and small-town Canada will become more reliant than ever before on our highway infrastructure. I urge this government to follow the leadership demonstrated by the Ontario government and allocate sufficient resources to the development of highways in northern Ontario. This government can no longer use the excuse that it is waiting for the province of Ontario to act. Ontario has taken positive action, positive action to the tune of $460 million for future highway expansion.
The onus is now on this government to reciprocate. Show your commitment to northern Ontario. Prove that you do have a total commitment to the north of this country.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Exploration Incentive Program was introduced on May 3, 1988.
The program was a response to the concerns expressed by the natural resources sector about the impact of two factors that may make things difficult for companies that try to raise new capital by issuing flow-through shares to finance exploration activities, and I am referring to the stock market crash in 1987 and tax reform.
The CEIP expires on December 31, 1990, and today I am worried about the survival of this program.
Mr. Speaker, the next federal budget is imminent, and we must ensure that the finance minister does not get rid of the CEIP in the next Budget.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Alliance for Trade and Job Opportunities has at long last decided to release a partial list of corporate donors that eagerly lined up to donate money to the free trade advertising extravaganza launched by big business in the last general election.
Contrary to earlier promises, this is not a complete list. Many American multinationals that were only too happy to go public with the support for the sell-out free trade deal have become surprisingly modest about releasing information about how much money they spent propping up the Tory Party. Companies refusing to release such information includes such huge U.S. companies as AT&T, GM and 3M. After shouting support for free trade from the roof-tops, why skulk in the closet about how much they spent supporting their Tory pals? Are they having an attack of conscience after seeing the disastrous effects of the deal on the Canadian economy? Or are they afraid to draw attention to themselves and endure the wrath of a duped Canadian public?
The most shameful aspect of this list is that every one of these huge corporations earned a tax deduction by donating vast sums to support the re-election of their cronies in the Tory Party. For example, Alcan contributed $250,000. Not only did this outstanding corporate citizen deduct every cent of this blatantly political contribution, but in 1986 the company managed to make so many tax deductions that it received a tax credit of $32 million after earning profits of $220 million. The Tory Party was so concerned about Alcan's measly profit of

$220 million that it decided to top it up with another $32 million of taxpayers' dollars.
