Mr. Speaker, December 7 was the second anniversary of the Patented Medicine Prices Review Board, created as a result of the 1987 amendments to the Patent Act, contained in Bill C-22.
With these amendments, our government intended to guarantee consumer access to drugs at reasonable prices, while at the same time providing an incentive to medical research in Canada. And those are exactly the results we are seeing today.
According to the first report, this new policy saved the Canadian consumer betwen $60 to $80 million last year.
Furthermore, during the first years the act to amend the Patent Act was in effect, the pharmaceutical industry invested over $72 million in research and development in Quebec, with Montreal benefiting most from these investments and the new jobs they generate.
Mr. Speaker, without those endless discussions by members of the opposition, especially by Liberal senators who did everything they could to prevent these changes from being enacted by Parliament, consumers, industry and workers in Quebec and across Canada would have enjoyed benefits much sooner.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday, December 10, was International Human Rights Day. It is therefore fitting to consider today the case of Reverend Laszlo Tokes of Romania.
Reverend Tokes is a well known religious leader and human rights advocate. Last year he boldly protested the "village destruction program" undertaken by his government. He has continued to knock on government doors and seek, through peaceful means, full enjoyment for all Romanian citizens of their right to private worship and community life.
For his determination to pursue his mission, he was evicted by his government from his congregation. Canada must persuade Romania to live up to its international responsibilities on human rights. Reverend Tokes, in fact all citizens of the world, have the right to practice their religion without fear of persecution.
I ask this government to take action to ensure that the Romanian government allow Reverend Tokes to continue to minister to his congregation. In the name of international solidarity, Canada must ensure that all citizens of the world be given their rightful place in their own country as we in our own land support the work of the Canadian Human Rights Commission.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to pay tribute today in this House to a distinguished Quebecer who has made a name for himself in tourism in the Quebec city area.
Mr. Speaker, Jacques du Sault has just been named president of Canada's Capital Visitors and Convention Bureau following a nation-wide competition in which more than 220 candidates competed this prestigious position.
Jacques du Sault will be able to bring together people on both sides of the river in Ottawa-Hull and pool

December 11, 1989
everyone's efforts in the National Capital Region for properly planned and coordinated tourism development.
He has been a hotel keeper, founding president of the Quebec City Region Tourism Board, president of the Tourism Committee of the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Metropolitan Quebec and director of the tourism development plan management committee for the greater Quebec region. His great personal experience, perfect bilingualism and desire to develop this beautiful region harmoniously will make Jacques du Sault an effective president.

Mr. Speaker, today in Montreal thousands of people are mourning the deaths of 14 women at the hands of a gun-toting madman. He was able to buy his semi-automatic rifle because he had met all legal requirements.
On Saturday, the Prime Minister said the ease with which Marc Lepine obtained his instrument of mass murder was "serious and unacceptable". He is quoted as saying his government would deal with the problem if necessary.
The fact that a man with serious psychological problems was able to legally obtain a powerful rifle and kill and wound more than two dozen innocent people should make it obvious even to the Prime Minister that action is necessary.
At the end of October, the Minister of Justice said he expected to bring in gun control legislation before Christmas. On Friday, the Solicitor General said it would be January or possibly later before legislation is tabled.
The time for action is now. We cannot wait for more innocent blood to be shed.

Mr. Speaker, may I ask this House to note the passing of a distinguished and scholarly Canadian gentleman. I refer to Robert Hamilton Hubbard who, until his sudden death this past November, served this nation in a quiet, unassuming and scholarly way, adding to our knowledge of ourselves as a nation and gently refining our view of the world.
It is not my intention to recite the details of Robert Hubbard's illustrious career, his entry into the Canadian Who's Who is almost four inches long, but to ask this House to note his passing and to acknowledge his aid to the ordinary business of Parliament.
I refer to the fact that the work of his later years; historian and cultural advisor to our governors general, and his unchallenged position as Canada's foremost art historian, made it an entirely natural matter to ask for his advice in an important artistic and cultural endeavour, such as the creation of national monuments.
As adviser to the committee formed to produce the splendid Diefenbaker monument that is engaged in similarly honouring Lester B. Pearson, Robert Hubbard will be missed both for the fine mind that he used to our benefit and for his gentlemanly and courteous demeanour which was a model to us all.

Mr. Speaker, since the government announced its disastrous decision to close CFB Summerside, Prince Edward Islanders have presented many valid objections but their protests continue to fall on deaf ears.
Now the Medical Society of Prince Edward Island says the relocation of the 413 Search and Rescue Squadron to CFB Greenwood will jeopardize the health and lives of islanders due to delays in medical evacuations to the mainland. Under the most ideal conditions, a one-hour delay in missions will occur. In bad weather, departures from Greenwood are time consuming and dangerous, whereas from Summerside they are safe and efficient.
Islanders are already isolated and therefore vulnerable. Why is this government deliberately exposing them to unnecessary delays in medical treatment resulting in distress, pain and even death? Islanders have a right to efficient medical services which means keeping the 413 Squadron at CFB Summerside.

Mr. Speaker,
. the carnage at the University of Montreal surely represents the manic edge of hatred and resentment by men against women achievers in non-traditional fields. Almost every woman in this House and other women who compete against men have experienced actions that reveal the misogyny that confronts women in universities, colleges, the workplace, the home, and on the streets of our nation. This hideously unjust desecration has brought home to most Canadians the need for action.
I urge the Prime Minister to establish a joint parliamentary committee to investigate violence against women, the harassment and the structural obstacles confronting women as we attempt to take our rightful place in society.
I also urge the Minister of Justice to bring forward gun control legislation to prohibit the sale or possession of automatic or semi-automatic weapons with the exception of those required by police forces. Lethal weapons should not be easily available to disturbed individuals. There should be no repetition of a mass killing such as the one in Montreal.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to express my concern over the grave and ominous future that confronts the tourism industry in the north. The futile and uncoordinated policies that this government has put forth will do nothing but decimate this key mechanism for northern development.
Tourism is perhaps Canada's biggest hidden industry, hidden to the tune of $21 billion per year. It plays a major role in stimulating northern development. Yet this government has done nothing to promote tourism in this country. On the contrary, with the cutbacks to VIA Rail and the impending goods and services tax, the government has come a long way in promoting tourism in other countries except our own. The loss of VIA Rail's Canadian route, combined with the loss of other northern routes, does not bode well for prospects for further development.
Oral Questions
The government has said that the GST will not affect tourism. However, the Conference Board of Canada estimates that $1 billion will be lost in 1991 alone and the Northern Ontario Tourist Outfitters Association has predicted a 20 per cent decline in tourism in the north. The government should be seizing every opportunity to expand this sector of the economy. When will this government give tourism the high priority status that it deserves?

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister and the Finance Minister have insisted that there will not be any major changes to the goods and services tax proposal. The minister said no tax on groceries, and some Conservative MPs said: "Well, let's try it". The minister said no to GST on existing housing, and the Blenkam report says: "Let's do it".
Now, in what has been described by some as a non-criminal leak, the government says: "No taxes on groceries, no taxes on existing housing, but a GST rate of 7 per cent".
Will the Finance Minister not wait this time for polling results and withdraw his crazy quilt patch-work proposal because Canadians are not prepared to take seven strokes of the tax whip any more than they are prepared to take nine strokes of the GST tax whip.
Mr. Speaker, I might take that particular suggestion more seriously if I had had any sort of alternative proposal from the Liberal party during the course of the last four months.
Scrap it.

The hon. member from Halifax says "scrap it". This is the sort of tax that we have been struggling with as a country for 65 years now. There was a Royal commission in 1940. There was another commission in 1955, another one in 1966, another one in 1973, and another one in 1983. All of them said: "Let's get rid of the tax". We have to move to a new type of sales tax system because the existing tax is hurting the economy.

Oral Questions
We are going to be proceeding with this tax. As the Prime Minister said, we will be making an announcement sometime before Christmas. As soon as I have the precise timing on that announcement, I will be advising the House.

Mr. Speaker, the federal government is now negotiating with the provinces, no doubt to force them to accept an agreement on a national sales tax. Does the government intend to force the provinces to accept a national sales tax by freezing transfer payments for post-secondary education and health care? My question to the Minister of Finance is this: Does he now intend to put through his goods and services tax on the backs of the provinces?

Mr. Speaker, it is not a
question of forcing the provinces to do anything. We had a meeting of federal and provincial finance ministers last Thursday. At that meeting there was a discussion of the goods and services tax. The provinces indicated there were a number of areas on which they wished to have further discussion. We have established a process, starting with meetings probably very early in January so we can pursue some of these concerns that the provinces have.
There is no question, there never has been a question, of whether or not we will force the provinces to do something. If they wish to join a national sales tax at some time in the future we have said all along that the door was open. There will be nothing done in the proposal, either in the design or in the implementation, to preclude that from happening.

Mr. Speaker, the government now has been dog-dancing around the goods and services tax proposal for quite some time. The minister just referred to whether or not there were any alternatives.
What I think would be interesting for Canadians to know is whether the Minister of Finance recognizes that he must focus on interest rates in this country that are up to 5 per cent higher than interest rates in the United States and on a Canadian dollar that has gone over 86
cents. Those two single things alone cause more damage to exports in Canada than anything that the MST has done over the years.
The question to the Minister of Finance is: After all this time spent on the goods and services taxes and all the flaws that are in it, is he prepared now to focus on doing something about the high interest rates and the high value of the Canadian dollar in this country to try to protect our export industries?

I think that the hon. member can only look back over the last five years to the number of statements I have made which recognize very clearly the importance of the export industry in this country and also the importance of having low interest rates.
We do have a problem of inflation in the country, a problem that is not just limited to certain parts of the country, but is growing more and more widespread across it. It is this problem that we feel we must deal with and we are going to deal with it, but that takes time. Unfortunately, it is taking longer than we expected because of the underlying strength in the economy. There are some signs that have appeared in the economic data over the last little while which indicate that there is some subsiding here, and hopefully there will be some time in the future when we can see lower interest rates.

Mr. Speaker, after months of hearing the Minister of Finance say that the goods and services tax rate could not be reduced from 9 per cent, Canadians are not going to be fooled by the suggestion of a 7 per cent rate. The Minister's problem, I suggest to him, is his own credibility.
No one believes that this government is not going to bring in the tax at one rate and increase it as soon as it gets a chance to do so. Canadians know that no matter what rate the GST is at the tax is going to be an administrative nightmare. They know that no matter what the rate is, it is not going to be visible. They know it is going to hurt the poor and the disadvantaged.
Why does the Minister not listen to what Canadians are saying and scrap this insane tax instead of sitting around listening to the pollsters trying to figure out how to hoodwink Canadians?
December 11, 1989

Mr. Speaker, there is so much that is wrong in the preamble of the hon. member's question that I do not know where to start. Let me make it clear.
The question has not been whether or not you can get an 8 per cent rate, a 7 per cent rate, or a 6 per cent rate. It is how you get to that rate, and that is where the difficult trade-offs come. This is what I have been pointing out time and time again. When people ask me that question on rate, I say there are very difficult trade-offs and the question that you have to respond to is what trade-offs are you prepared to make.
We had some useful suggestions from the Conservative members of the finance committee. We got absolutely nothing from the Liberal Party of Canada as to how we might get the rate down. As I replied in answer to one of the earlier questions, it strikes me as very unusual that we should have this posturing on the part of Liberal members when they have done absolutely nothing to contribute to the dialogue and the debate that is going to result in a better sales tax system in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I turn the minister's words back to him. The problem with the GST is that it is such a mess it is hard to know where to start to criticize it.
The government is proposing to replace a tax, which is currently paid by about 75,000 firms, with one that is going to be collected by about 1.25 million firms, and most of them are going to file monthly forms. Whatever the rate, Canada is going to be the only developed country in the world with a two-tier retail tax, and the minister will enjoy the distinction of having introduced the single most complex fiscal measure in Canada's history.
Will the minister not admit that implementing the GST in January, 1991, will be an administrative fiasco and the only reason for his obsession with this date is that he hopes election.

Mr. Speaker, at some time governments have to decide on these major issues and do something.
As I indicated in response to an earlier question, the Liberal party looked at five consecutive reports every ten years and ignored each one of them. Each time a report came back it stated: "Get rid of the manufacturers' sales
Oral Questions
tax." The point is that at the time when we know there is a tax that is a bad tax for the country, it must be removed and we are going to remove it.
The hon. member said there are only 75,000 people who pay the tax directly, but indirectly every Canadian consumer pays the existing federal sales tax. But it is invisible. No one knows that it is there. In response to my friend from Gloucester, this tax is going to be a very visible tax. There will not be one person in the country who will not be aware that there is a goods and services tax, and that is accountability. For years and years the Liberal party ignored the fact that the existing tax is hidden. This is one of the things we are going to change because it brings about better accountability in government.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Government figures for next year's farm net income show declines of 54 per cent in the province of Alberta, declines of 87 per cent in Manitoba, and a whopping decline of 101 per cent in Saskatchewan. His anti-inflation program seems to have wiped out farm incomes altogether on the prairies.
Farm families have no unemployment insurance, they are not eligible for welfare, and other safety nets miss them as well. Since they will not have enough income to pay cash costs, let alone something to support families and make capital payments, what does the government intend to do?

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Agriculture has addressed that question in the House. There is a major conference on today and tomorrow that will involve discussion of that very question. I expect that the more appropriate time to respond to that question is after the consultation has occurred, after the Minister of Agriculture has listened to the concerns of the farming community. After that we can make some decisions.

Mr. Speaker, global farm production has failed to meet global demand in three consecutive years. Yet, Canadian grain prices are lower this year than last year. Will the Minister of Finance abandon his high

Oral Questions
interest rate, high dollar policy to allow farmers to reduce their input costs and increase the export value of their grain?
Mr. Speaker, I think if the hon. member reflects on the purpose of the goods and services tax, he will see that that is a means by which all farmers can remove the tax on all of their-
That wasn't the question.

The hon. member is shaking his head. Clearly, the hon. member does not understand what the goods and services tax is all about. It will allow the farmer to remove all forms of taxes on all business inputs into the farming operation.
The hon. member has raised the question of interest rates. If he thinks back to 1980-81-82, at a time when interest rates were very high in this country, it was because the government of the day forgot and ignored the whole question of inflation that was building through the course of the seventies-
You wiped out income.

It did not address the problem, and the result was the blow-off of high inflation of 13 per cent, high interest rates of about 20 per cent to 25 per cent and the tremendous disaster which resulted from that. That is what we are trying to avoid. We understand that there are concerns which are being expressed now, but if we do not address this problem we are going to get right back into the mess-
No income is not inflationary.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member can only yell. If he could listen a bit, he might learn something.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Agriculture, I will also direct my question to the Minister of Finance. Article 703 of the free trade agreement states that in order to facilitate trade in agricultural goods, Canada and the United States shall work together to eliminate what is termed "restrictive trade barriers". Given the fact that supply management programs are under heavy attack during the current GATT negotiations and also by the international Cairns Group, constituting what we could define as "restrictive trade barriers", will the minister agree that the future of Canada's supply management systems under the provisions of the free trade agreement in fact hinges on our successful performance at these negotiations?
Second, will the minister specify what actions his government is prepared to initiate and to take to ensure that our supply management systems, as we know them today, are going to be maintained?

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to respond to the hon. member, especially at a time like this when we have so many farmers and agri-food people in Ottawa to attend a conference. The member addressed supply management. Part of that meeting is devoted particularly to supply management, where these issues will be addressed. Mr. Speaker, the fact that violence in the media contributes to violence against women is accepted by virtually all experts. Twice this government has introduced legislation against pornography and twice has had to withdraw it.
My question is directed to the Minister of Justice. Will the minister undertake today to bring in legislation against pornography that includes sanctions against violence, violence outside of sexual context, in movies, television, videos and magazines?

problem of pornography. It included child pornography, violence and all sorts of pornography.

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Finance. Transportation is a key factor to Canada's economic and social well-being. It is the life line I would suggest to all the outlying regions of our country. Yet the proposed goods and services tax will apply to all transportation costs whether it be at 9 per cent, 7 per cent or any per cent. Northerners will pay more. They will pay more for the snowsuits for their children. They will pay more for their heating bills and they will pay more for all other necessities of life because transportation costs will be built in, and those are higher.
Oral Questions
Will the minister admit that the goods and services tax discriminates against people in outlying regions? What does he propose to do about it?

Mr. Speaker, first of all, let me say very clearly that the tax on transportation cost is removed by the particular design of the goods and services tax so that there is no tax on the transportation cost.
The hon. member is expressing some surprise on that. I would suggest that she learn how the tax is designed to remove the tax from all business inputs, and one of those inputs is transportation costs. The hon. member has zeroed in on one aspect of the tax but I think it is very clear in the economic analysis that has been done that the regions of the country, because they normally depend more on exports, normally depend on very capital intensive industries, are beneficiaries of the goods and services tax. That is why the regions of the country benefit more than parts of the country like southern Ontario or southern Quebec. That comes from the nature of the tax itself.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot believe this. The Minister of Finance does not understand his own tax. Since when does a vendor pay a cost of transportation and not add it into the cost that he charges to the consumer? When you buy a refrigerator in northern Ontario, do you not pay for the transportation costs in the final price, and then there is a tax?
What will the minister do to offset this double whammy to people who live away from the major centres? Maybe he should study his own tax.

Mr. Speaker I think that I understand the tax having sat around boardroom tables and talked to people from coast to coast to coast on the nature of this tax. I think I do understand how the tax is constructed.
Let me again go back to the comments that the hon. member has raised. There is no question that transportation costs are one of the costs in a product that is consumed in any part of the country. That is only one part of the cost. There are other costs that are part of the over-all cost of the product that is consumed but the key here is that you have to look at the broad benefit, the

broad impact of the tax to different parts of the country as opposed to identifying one particular element of it.

You have to look at the broad impact of the tax and that is where the economic analysis says that the regions of the country are greater beneficiaries than is the case in the more developed areas of southwestern Ontario.

Why has the government done nothing after six months of having a special committee? Why has it done nothing to keep those plants going, even on a part-time basis?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no words exchanged in this House could capture the distress that families are going to feel as a result of the decisions announced by National Sea Products this morning. These decisions affect the communities of Canso, St. John's and North Sydney as well.
It is true to say that the government has not announced a major package of initiatives to date but we do recognize the serious dilemma facing the groundfish sector in Atlantic Canada. We are very much in tune with the needs, sentiments and anxieties of the people living in communities affected by these matters.
That is why my colleagues, the Minister for International Trade and the Minister for Public Works, in Canso and St. John's East this morning announced major initiatives in the area of industrial adjustment and industrial diversification. There will be further information to follow, as appropriate.

Mr. Speaker, the minister completely ignored the question. The government has had a special committee of cabinet for six months. No announcements have been made. They have known for weeks and weeks and weeks that these closures would be occurring. Why has the government done nothing to maintain the jobs in those communities? Why has it done absolutely nothing?

Mr. Speaker, it is not true to suggest that anyone has known for weeks and weeks that specific communities would be impacted by specific decisions.
These are decisions that are taken by the corporate side and they depend very heavily on the circumstances in the market-place and with respect to resource supply. I repeat that the government is taking measures to ensure that there is a bright future, that there are in many cases alternatives and in some cases alternatives within the fishery in order that these communities can continue to to survive and prosper as this government would intend to be the case.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Justice. Since November 29, Richard Bilodeau, a Canadian living in my riding, has been detained in prison in New Hampshire, in the United States, following an automobile accident in which three people were killed. U.S. authorities object to his release. They claim, on the basis of a written opinion by the U.S. Department of Justice, that the extradition treaty between Canada and the United States does not apply in the case of manslaughter and criminal negligence, when such offences are committed while driving a car. The district attorneys of the State of New Hampshire are concerned about the possibility that Canadian authorities might not observe the extradition treaty.
Clearly, Mr. Bilodeau's rights, are not being respected, and he has every right to our support and assistance.
Could the Minister of Justice reaffirm his confidence in the extradition treaty between Canada and the United States, and re-establish the facts with respect to its scope and eventual compliance with the treaty? Furthermore, could the minister reassure Mr. Bilodeau's family and

contact the U.S. Department of Justice to ensure that his rights are respected?

Mr. Speaker, I will take this question, if I may, on behalf of the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
The extradition treaty which is in effect between Canada and the United States does apply to this type of situation. The government is aware of Mr. Bilodeau's case and his difficulties in New Hampshire. We are following the situation carefully. I am sure the United States of America and the courts in that state will preserve Mr. Bilodeau's rights. I understand that the matter should be solved shortly.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. It is indeed a sad day for Atlantic Canada, especially for the workers in St. John's and Canso. There will be over 1,500 jobs lost and in the case of Canso, a loss of 750 jobs means the closure of the community. This government cannot allow this closure to go ahead without proper plans and proper programs to save the community.
What considerations were given by this government for the people and the workers of that community. Did the bottom line of National Sea Products weigh more than all those people put together in those communities?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is very important to know that the government will be very concerned with the workers and with the communities. That is our first concern.
There are a number of things under way as the Minister for International Trade and the Minister of Public Works announced this morning. First of all, we are ensuring in the short term that all of the workers will qualify for unemployment insurance and if they do not that they will obtain sufficient weeks of work to qualify. Second, there is a particular concern for older workers
Oral Questions
and the Older Workers Adjustment Program will apply in this case. Third, there is a community development fund that will be a significant step for the communities which are affected in terms of helping them to build a future.
It was also said this morning in our announcement that the level of funding will be determined by the size of the lay-offs and the needs of each community because we want to ensure that each community is looked at individually.

This still means that the plant will be closing.
How can we really be sure that the government has looked at all the options for keeping the Canso plant open? Why did National Sea announce all these cutbacks even before the fisheries plan for 1990 was published? My question is as follows: Is the government an accomplice in all these lay-offs and plant closings?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is certainly not the case. My colleagues who have sat and discussed these pending developments without knowing which specific communities would be hit and to what degree have wrestled intensely for several months with the dilemma posed to a number of communities in Atlantic Canada, not only because of the market factors I mentioned but also because of the deteriorating abundance of supply to these plants.
The question then arose as to whether a number of plants could be kept open by operating on such a marginal basis that they no longer became economic and viable. We decided that those decisions in the final analysis were best left to the private sector but that the government would move in with the full strength of resources to look after the needs of people, to look after the rejuvenation of these communities. My colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, will in the days ahead be giving further detail on how we intend to do that.

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Finance. At the end of October the northern tax benefits report was made public. If the recommendations are implemented as proposed, some 72 communities in northern Ontario will lose this benefit and drain some $5 million from the economy. Some of the communities like Marathon, Terrace Bay, Schreiber and Geraldton should also have qualified.
Considering that seven sawmills have closed and 2,000 jobs have been lost already, can the minister assure this House and northern Ontarians that he will totally reject the report's recommendation?

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member has said, the report was made available some time toward the end of October. We have been reviewing this report and are continuing to do that work. At this point I do not have any statement as to what the government's position will be.
We appreciate the work that was done by that task force, a task force composed of people who live in isolated communities and who spent a good deal of time going around the country understanding the problems and trying to come up with a proposal that was an equitable and stable proposal. That is the result that they have presented to the government.
As I said, we are studying this now and I hope that not too far down the road we will have a decision.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister for International Trade, I have a question for the Minister of Forestry that also deals with the serious northern Ontario problem.
It seems contradictory that on the one hand the government claims that the manufacturers' sales tax is hurting Canadian exports and uses this as a rationale for introducing the goods and services tax, yet this government has turned around and hit our forestry sector with a 15 per cent export surtax in this era of so-called free trade.
In view of the fact that our dollar has reached a 10-year high, making our exports less competitive, when will this government stop sabotaging our primary resource industries and ensure that we are competing on a level playing field?

Mr. Speaker, we are, of course, sensitive to the difficulties of this particular industry, particularly in northern Ontario. A number of factors are at play, including the fibre supply situation, the exchange rate and perhaps, more important, a decline in housing starts in the United States. All of these are important factors.
The hon. member knows that it would be up to the province of Ontario principally to propose, as other provinces have done, that certain offsets be required before this particular tax can be eliminated.
Let us not forget that the tax does not accrue to an American jurisdiction, but accrues to the province of Ontario which, of course, has the option to return some of this money back to the resource in northern Ontario.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
On Saturday the Prime Minister announced that the government was prepared to drop the rate of the proposed GST to 7 per cent through major spending cuts of up to $6 billion per year. This promise carries an implied threat. Since the 1988 election we have seen the elimination of universality in our social programs, further cuts to health care and education, cuts in regional development, the gutting of VIA Rail, the removal of government financing of the UI program and the lay-off of tens of thousands of Canadians.
Will the Minister of Finance confirm that the proposal to reduce the proposed rate to 7 per cent will mean further massive cuts to programs affecting Canadians and will he tell us where he plans to cut back?

Mr. Speaker, I think that the preamble to the hon. member's statement was as loaded with inaccuracies as I have heard in any preamble since I have been in the House.

The Prime Minister did not say that. He did indicate that there would be some spending cuts over the course of the next little while. I think the hon. member, if she is listening to people in Canada, will find that they are concerned about the debt. They are concerned about the level of government spending. They are concerned about the level of taxation.
Canadians want to be assured that we are spending taxpayers' dollars as effectively and as efficiently as possible. They also want to know that we are doing everything we can to get the level of debt down so that we are not carrying over to future generations a very heavy burden of trying to support that debt.
This is what we have been trying to do since November 1984 and we are going to continue to do that because we understand the significance of debt control in the future health of this country and in our ability to be able to maintain the programs that Canadians value.

Mr. Speaker, the finance minister maintains the pretence that the GST is inevitable and he has said again today in this House that he has no intention of withdrawing it.
I think he has already answered this question but I am going to put it so I can get it straight from him. Is it not the strategy of this government to feed the anxiety over the federal deficit in order to sell this regressive sales tax?

Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is a question of feeding any anxieties. It is simply a question of reading the facts. The facts are there. The debt in this country is too high. It must be controlled. The deficit when we came in was $38 billion. We got it down to $28.7 billion last year, but that is still too high. It means that we have to continue to control government spending. That is the best way-
What about interest rates?

The hon. member throws in another question. Possibly she could get it all together and put the question to me at one time and I will give her the answer she wants.

speakeroldname: Mr. John A. MacDougall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take a few moments just to review Bill C-4. Just over ten years ago, the Energy Supplies Emergency Act was put into place to ensure that Canada has an appropriate contingency plan in place to deal with any possible disruption in the international oil market.
As a result of the oil market crisis in 1973 and 1974, Canada became a party to the agreement of an international energy program which is administered by the International Energy Agency, the IEA. Through the IEA, 21 nation members are joined in planning for their collective energy and economic security.
The Energy Supplies Emergency Act established the Energy Supplies Allocation Board, ESAB, and made it responsible for Canada's fulfilment of the act's objectives and programs.
The act underwent a series of amendments in 1982 to improve the allocation and rationing programs. Again the government is advancing another series of housekeeping amendments in Bill C-4 to overcome operational problems which the industry and the board together have identified.
Government Orders
I will very briefly review the clauses of this bill. Clause 1 amends the definition of the wholesale consumer to include owners of homes, farms and small businesses and thus ensure their fair share of available supplies in case of allocation or rationing.
Clause 2 amends the composition of the Energy Supplies Allocation Board, removing Petro-Canada's membership from the board. Since its appointment to the board over a decade ago, Petro-Canada has evolved from being an instrument of public policy to becoming a major competitor in the market-place. It is now an inappropriate time to have Petro-Canada represented on the board, given the confidentiality of information supplied to the board and the control which the board would exercise on the marketing side of the petroleum industry, in the event of a declared emergency. This amendment is designed to remove Petro-Canada's conflict of interest.
In line with the Clause 2, amendment Clause 3 replaces Petro-Canada on the international agency's standing group on emergency questions with a senior official from ESAB or Energy, Mines and Resources.
Clause 4 removes an ambiguity in relation to ESAB's powers to regulate wholesale prices in an allocation program. It authorizes the board to set the manner for determining wholesale prices for controlled products. This is in addition to the existing authority to set prices or a range of prices and would allow ESAB to be sensitive to market forces.
Clause 5(1) would provide flexibility to ESAB to use any department or agency of the Government of Canada including Canada Post Corporation to distribute, return and account for rationing documents.
Clause 5(2) extends the powers of ESAB to regulate rather than prescribe retail prices under the rationing programs.
Clause 5(3) would allow financial institutions under provincial authority, for example, credit unions and caisse populates, to participate in the delivery of the rationing program along with banks and trust companies.
Clause 6 relates to the contractual supply obligations at the time of allocation and rationing. This amendment would make clear that contracts would remain in force despite price changes arising from the board's regulation in times of emergency.

Clause 7 concerns petroleum companies and their role in ESAB. During a national emergency, it is essential that companies be able to discuss their supply situation at meetings of the petroleum industry advisory committee. This is made possible by exemption from the Competition Act. The amendment simply extends the protection under the Competition Act from 12 months to 24 months in order to save time and effort, as the process of obtaining the exemption involves a number of months each time.
Clause 8 would place a duty of confidentiality on ESAB, its officers, its independent contractors, agents and employees assigned to it. It further provides that confidential information may not be released for legal proceedings except for administration and enforcement of this act and for criminal proceedings under an act of Parliament.
As a consequence of adopting the aforementioned amendment of confidentiality of information, Clause 9 amends the schedule to the Access to Information Act by adding the Energy Supplies Emergency Act.
The need for Canada to maintain its state of preparedness against a possible petroleum emergency continues to be an important component of Canadian energy policy. The bill before the House today is simply a further step in the process of strengthening the provisions of the Energy Supplies Emergency Act so that they may be more effectively implemented in the future.
I would like to thank the members of the committee on all sides for the work that they have done.

The reason we are so concerned about this happening is that once shares are privately owned, the policies of that company will serve the interests of the shareholders and not necessarily the interests of Government of Canada or the interests of Canadians. If it ever happened that Petro-Canada was privatized, concerns with profit could come before concerns with the environment, with energy self-sufficiency and with security of supply. This would remove options the government and all Canadians now have regarding their energy future.
I also have concerns about whether there will be a full and frank debate on the merits of privatization or whether the government will go blindly ahead as it did on other issues. The VIA Rail issue comes to mind as one example of this. In this instance, the government refused to listen to Canadians and even to Parliament. Instead, it chose to follow a policy that suited its own political interests. So will a Petro-Canada debate be another example of this arrogance? I certainly hope not.
The other concern I have with regard to privatization is the sale of Canada Post. In my province of Prince Edward Island and in other areas of rural Canada, post offices have been shut down because of this government's policy. In Clause 5 of this bill, the government continues that process by removing Canada Post from the plan and allowing other government agencies to perform functions that would have been performed by the post office.
By removing the reference to Canada Post, the government is signalling a third change of plans for the post office. By nudging Canada Post even further along the path of privatization, this government is putting more rural post offices at risk. In so doing, it is putting a way of life in rural communities at risk as well.
Another important issue raised by this bill is the free trade agreement. As we know, this deal makes it possible for the United States to continue to receive energy from Canada while Canadians are being forced to cut back. Under Article 904 of the agreement, if Canada wants to
Government Orders
cut back its energy exports to the United States, it must first cut back supplies to Canadians.
The amount we keep from the Americans is just a drop in the bucket by their standards, but the amount that we deprive our fellow Canadians of may be much more serious. In a country like Canada with a cold climate, energy reductions could have major effects. If Canada proceeds with energy conservation and energy efficiency in an effort to protect the environment, the room for cutting back will be even smaller. That is another reason to safeguard our energy supply.
We think that the trade deal fails to do this. Instead, what it does is it puts at risk Canada's future energy security. As we see it, Canada's energy bounty should benefit Canadians first and Americans second. We are not convinced that the free trade agreement follows that philosophy.
The Minister of Energy has said that Canada's obligations under the international energy agreement are more demanding than those under the free trade agreement, and therefore we should not be worried about the FTA, but rather the IEA. But as the minister knows, the free trade agreement governs trade in normal as well as emergency situations. So that argument really does not convey the whole picture.
Under the international energy agreement, Canada is obliged to share up to 7 per cent of its oil with other countries at the time of international disruption. The free trade agreement does nothing to limit our obligations. In fact, it increases them by extending our obligations to non-emergency situations as well.
I would like to comment briefly on the context into which Bill C-4 fits, and what this government should be doing in this regard in the future.
As we all know, major disruptions in the oil supply do not occur every day. The last two, in 1972-73, and in 1978-79, were due to international conflicts concerning oil-producing countries. But the world today is not the same as it was 20, 10 or even one year ago. Major political, economic and social changes have taken place which bode well for the future.
The dismantling of the Berlin wall, for example, is just one event, but it symbolizes the whole easing of tensions between east and west. Canadians can be encouraged by

December 11, 1989
Government Orders
such events. In fact, a recent poll by the Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security found that Canadians today consider environmental and economic threats to be more serious than military threats. When asked what will be the pressing concerns in the year 2000, Canadians ranked the environment even higher.
I think the lesson that we learn here is that the government should be stressing the environment in its policies. Oil spills, not oil shocks, are threatening to become the real energy emergency issue in the future.
This government has been slow to respond to environmental issues which threaten not only our energy future, but our very survival as well. For example, the government has cut back spending on conservation and alternative energy from $410 million in 1984-85, to $49 million in 1989-90. In my province of Prince Edward Island, the federal energy conservation office has been closed. The same is true all across this country.
These programs help provinces like mine diversify their energy mix and become less dependent on oil. In Prince Edward Island, we are trying to do this by using biomass fuel. In doing so, we are not only helping the environment and getting ourselves off oil, we are also creating jobs.
The federal government would do well to assist provinces like Prince Edward Island generate industries which not only reduce our dependency on oil, but on federal transfer payments as well.
I would urge this government to prepare for the real energy emergency in the future, and of right now, the environment. It should be listening to Canadians on environmental issues, working within the IEA to push for global action on the environment. Opponents of measures such as carbon tax have argued there is no point in putting a carbon tax on fuel sold to Canadians while fuels sold in the United States and elsewhere are not similarly taxed. This would only hurt Canadians, they argue.
I suggest by working within the IEA and within other organizations, the government could push for measures by all countries so that both Canadians and the environment come out on top. Mr. Speaker, that generally covers my concerns about the issues raised in and by Bill C-4.
I just want to conclude by saying that while I am pleased that the government is taking steps to prepare for emergencies, I have some serious concerns about how it is doing so.

She said: Mr. Speaker, it is important to note that we are debating Bill C-23, an act to amend the National Energy Board Act. This year is the thirtieth anniversary of that board, an organization that has served Canada extremely well and one which has developed a reputation as a defender of the national interest in energy matters, no matter which way the political winds happen to be blowing.
The board's solid reputation and the importance to Canada of not hurting that reputation means that any amendments to the board's legislation must be made with great care. The government has not done this with Bill C-23. Witness after witness at the standing committee poked holes in the government's arguments concerning C-23 and from that committee I come with the amendments that I am proposing today.
I would like to explain and defend the motions before you, Mr. Speaker, regarding Bill C-23. Motion No. 1 deals with international power lines. This group of amendments would accomplish several things. First, it would eliminate the potential for most kinds of political interference by the cabinet in the regulation of electric-

Government Orders
ity and also in matters that rightly belong under the jurisdiction of the non-partisan National Energy Board.
As you know, right now, when the board receives an application for a power line application, it automatically holds a public hearing. But that will no longer be the case. Under Bill C-23 the board will have to ask the federal cabinet for permission to hold that hearing. Mr. Speaker, we disagree with that kind of interference which the government could use to further its own political agenda at the expense of the national interest. This motion would eliminate that by giving the board the power to call a hearing.
Also, with this amendment the National Energy Board would do a better job of protecting the environment from the effects of electrical production and export. It would do this by assigning to FEARO, the Federal Environmental Assessment Review Office, the task of helping to assess an application to the National Energy Board for environmental effects. It would do so in the context of providing a second opinion for the NEB to consider.
As it stands now, the environmental team at the board look at the applications for environmental effects. We feel that the House of Commons should be able to call on the Minister of the Environment to account for what the government is doing to safeguard the environment, and this amendment will allow the House of Commons to do that.
Bill C-23, as it is presently worded, allows the Governor in Council certain unwarranted powers. These powers include deciding whether there will be a hearing on electricity export or power line projects, setting the criteria for whether the National Energy Board recommends a hearing and deciding what the NEB will examine at the hearing.
At the Standing Committee hearings we heard mainly negative comments on these sections which give a good measure of power to a political body, the federal cabinet. From Nova Scotia Power we heard:
These provisions interject too much uncertainty into the process
and could serve to discourage exports.
New Brunswick Power said that through Bill C-23 the government is:
- transferring a jurisdiction away from an independent and impartial National Energy Board, according to well-defined legal rules, and giving it to the cabinet to be exercised according to no rules whatsoever.
We agree with what New Brunswick Power has said because we feel that the decision as to whether that public inquiry should be held should be the decision of the National Energy Board and not the cabinet.
I would, in fact, suggest that the government take the wise advice of the Quebec Cree who said: "Bill C-23 must be completely rewritten". The Cree of Quebec are veiy concerned about the prospect for public hearings if Bill C-23 passes, and they are concerned with good reason.
At this point I would like to refer to a statement by one of the government members of our committee who expressed his confidence in the bill. He said:
If I thought that (the) opportunity (for hearings) was not there, for
anyone in Canada, I would be the first one to demand changes.
I shall attempt to prove to you today, Mr. Speaker, that that opportunity will likely not be there. I hope that afterwards the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Energy will honour his word and support this motion.
I would like to begin by taking a moment to compare the National Energy Board to the Federal Court of Canada. The Federal Court has greater powers than the National Energy Board and its rulings are binding. The court's advice to the cabinet is open to the public as the National Energy Board's advice to the government would be in the case of an export of electricity or power line application. The public, including groups like the Quebec Cree, has a chance to go before the court and make its case.
In a recent case the Cree went before the court to demand hearings on the James Bay hydro project. Despite a court precedent against them regarding a Saskatchewan dam project, despite the fact that everything was made public, the government still refused, until this fall, to allow a public hearing on James Bay. Even the way the government arranged the hearing was objectionable, for it violated both the spirit and the word of the 1975 James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement.
This agreement requires that the Cree be involved in any discussions on the James Bay project including those leading to an environmental review. Talks were held between Ottawa and Quebec but they excluded the Cree. After months of foot dragging and after being dragged through the courts, the federal government probably feared it would face the embarrassment of being ordered by the court to call a hearing so at the last
December 11, 1989

minute it agreed to a joint public hearing with the province of Quebec.
If this bill passes as it is, it is going to be very difficult every time for the National Energy Board to convince the cabinet to allow a public hearing. We can only look at other examples in the government's record. As stated earlier, in the case of the Saskatchewan dam project the Minister of the Environment was shown to have failed to implement his own guidelines. If we take the decision to shut down or cut back on VIA Rail we find that no public hearings on environmental effects on the decisions were held, let alone hearings on economic or social effects.
The government just decided to shut down or cut back parts of VIA Rail. It made that decision without any public discussion, with no concern whatsoever as to how this decision would affect the people of Canada. If we look at the record of the government we can easily see why the Cree would be concerned about public hearings.
I know that my time is about up. I have further arguments to make on other amendments which I will put forward later. I want to conclude my remarks on the first motion by saying that Bill C-23 gives too much power to the cabinet. We are proposing this amendment so that the National Energy Board, not the cabinet, will decide if a public enquiry is necessary.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise in the House today to speak on the first group of amendments to Bill C-23, an Act to amend the National Energy Board Act. My colleague from Malpeque would know that my hon. friend from Edmonton East, who is our energy critic, has done a considerable amount of work on this legislation. I know he brings considerable expertise to this House and to this party, being the first New Democrat elected to this House from the great Province of Alberta.
In committee a great deal of work was done in studying this legislation and many of the concerns were raised by my colleague, and we rise here today to support the amendments that are being brought forward by the hon. member from Malpeque. In fact, if I am not mistaken, most of these amendments were presented in the committee in its legislative review of the bill. Unfortunately, the government refused to accept them and we are here
Government Orders
today in one final effort to try to improve this legislation. We hope that with our convincing arguments we will be able to have the government support our view with regard to the changes that are required to this legislation.
Let us take a look at the general problem we have with Bill C-23. In our view it undermines the National Energy Board, politicizes the decisions, makes the exports of a strategic resource easier, public hearings will become more rare, and environmental concerns, already given short shrift by this government, will receive even less attention in the future.
One of the principal concerns we have with this bill is that the final decision on whether or not a public hearing is held on the construction of a power line or the export of electricity is made by the cabinet and not the National Energy Board. With the passage of Bill C-23, these decisions would be much more likely to be made on narrow political grounds. We know the reasons we have argued in this House for independent bodies. We argue for those to make sure that, as much as possible, the decisions that are made are made in the best interests of that particular sphere and in this country, not just for cheap political gains as has all too often become the case with the government opposite.
During second reading, my colleague from Edmonton East pointed out how this could easily result in the national interest being poorly protected and in the interest of a small province being unfairly trampled by a cabinet trying to please a large province, something we all know about from the federal election.
We pointed out that the authority of the National Energy Board itself could be seriously undermined if cabinet decided to override a recommendation by the NEB merely for political reasons. We also pointed out that under the changes in this bill the National Energy Board will routinely approve applications for power lines and electricity exports. As a result, in the vast majority of cases public hearings will not be held.
Well, what have we proposed? We proposed a system of licensing power lines and electricity exports that had at its core the notion of prudence. The hon. member from Edmonton East is a man of great prudence and he

December 11, 1989
Government Orders
considered this strongly when he was making these suggestions in committee.
For example, we are hearing now that the Government of Ontario is speaking of future electricity shortages although some people are in fact suggesting that this is mere manipulation by the Liberal government in Ontario, in effect, to implement what would appear to be a shoddy electrical generation procedure and policy already in place and, of course, to whip up support for future nuclear projects.
We heard evidence from the province of Quebec before the energy committee the other day that hydro reservoirs are much lower than normal. We are hearing from climatologists that global warming will likely change weather patterns and that this could affect rainfall and the viability of certain hydroelectric facilities. We are hearing further from Canadians all across this country, on television and in the newspapers, that Canadians are deeply concerned about the environment and they want public officials, government, to take real action and not just spout rhetoric.
I have no doubt that south of the border demand for electricity will increase in the future, partly because the pollution it causes is emitted mainly where electricity is produced rather than where it is used. I think that is an important point to remember. Our approach in dealing with this increasingly strategic Canadian resource is to be prudent. I come from the province of British Columbia where electricity is considered a resource by the provincial government and one that we must take pains to ensure that we develop properly in environmentally sound ways. The key is to be prudent.
We believe that the Governor in Council, the cabinet, should act not as an accelerator for the National Energy Board but as a brake of last resort. That is why my colleague proposed in committee that if the NEB refused a proposal to build a power line or to export electricity that that would be the end of it, the cabinet could not overrule a refusal by the NEB. On the other hand, if the NEB accepted such a proposal the cabinet could still review and overturn the NEB decision. This would have the effect of protecting the national interest by having a double check on electricity projects and exports.
Let us take a look at some of the proposals presented by the Liberals. The amendments proposed in this package do not go that far, but they do proceed in the right direction. These amendments would have the effect of helping to protect the independence of the NEB and we support that. Protecting the NEB's independence may not be the main aim of the amendments but that is the effect that they would have.
We believe that the National Energy Board should be able to make the decision on its own, without interference from the cabinet, about which power projects should receive close environmental scrutiny, and in the case of these amendments, by the Federal Environmental Assessment Review Office. We learned just last week that, in fact, legislation on a legislative environmental assessment review process has yet to even make its way to cabinet ministers or into the cabinet. That gives rise to concern among many people about, again, the ongoing rhetoric from the government and no real action being taken.
We also believe that the environmental consequences of public policy must be considered much more fully than is currently the case. This is especially true for energy policy. More and more Canadians recognize the environmental consequences of energy consumption; flooding valleys when hydro dams are built, trying to manage nuclear waste, adding to the greenhouse effect-you name it. Canadians are more and more concerned about the environmental consequences of energy generation.
When it comes to power lines, there is great concern on Vancouver Island over this matter. Scientists from either side are lining up to present their arguments as to the impact and effect on not only the health of all of us but the health, in many cases, of farm animals.
There is an argument to be made that the role of the NEB and other regulatory bodies should include environmental reviews as part of their mandate. This bill goes some way toward that but we need a great deal more impact when it comes to the legislative environmental process that has been promised by this government.
We are looking forward to the debate on this bill. I know my colleague from Edmonton East has done a considerable amount of work on this. We will be supporting the amendments as proposed by the hon. member from Malpeque and I hope the government will listen
December 11, 1989

today so that we can ensure that we get better legislation out of this proposal.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of the fine intervention by my colleague from Malpeque and the arguments that she made in connection with the importance of public hearings. Before I do that, however, I would like to point out that this bill is another measure down the slippery road that we have undertaken by way of the free trade agreement.
I would like to draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, particularly to Division III and section 119.5 which commits ourselves and forces the National Energy Board to commit itself to the overall energy agreement with the United States which we opposed in the last election and which we continue to consider to be detrimental to our national interest.
For that reason alone, we must rise in this House and oppose it because we do not think that the long-term interest of Canada is served by taking us down this slippery road in connection with our long-term energy interest because of the commitment that was made, unfortunately, under the free trade agreement which in the last election, of course, we opposed.
Bill C-23 is another example of a bill prepared without sustainable development and the long term in mind. Despite the proclamations, commitments and statements that the Prime Minister of Canada makes abroad, despite the commitments that the Environment Minister makes in his speeches at the UN and when he appears before the Environment Committee, here we have a bill that restricts even further the powers of an institution that has served Canada well, namely the National Energy Board, and says that we will let cabinets of the future make certain decisions, but you as a board should have less and less power.
What does that mean? We all know that cabinets have, by virtue of their political nature, so to speak, short-term sights. They can think at best, under the best of circumstances, of the next election. To think beyond that requires a supernatural effort, let alone thinking of the next generation and generations after. By that I mean the long term, 50, 60, 100 years from now. That is why the National Energy Board was formed and that is why a
Government Orders
stronger National Energy Board is necessary and not a weaker one.
Here we have, in the name, allegedly, of sustainable development as interpreted by the Progressive Conservative government, a bill coming into the House which weakens instead of strengthening the National Energy Board. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, does that make sense to you? That is one reason alone to oppose it in addition to the other one I gave you a moment earlier, namely, Division III, the section related to the free trade agreement.
The importance of holding public hearings, and not at the whim of cabinet, has been eloquently described and underlined by the member for Malpeque. Of course we all agree with her. We know that that should not be a political decision of the day. It should be an established practice because we know the importance of seeking public consultation.
I cannot for the life of me understand, considering the commitments that the Progressive Conservative Party made in the election of 1984, proclaiming its great belief in consultation with the people, that the government would come into the House with this bill today and practise exactly the opposite, as it does in Bill C-23. It is inconceivable, it runs counter to all the commitments made in public at election time by the Progressive Conservative Party.
If anything, the National Energy Board should retain that function. It should not be made a decision of cabinet because we know what the political pitfalls are of that process. If anything, the powers of the National Energy Board to hold public hearings should be strengthened.
But what is worrisome about the long-term implications of this bill is the mindset in the political philosophy behind it because it reinforces the destiny of Canada as a provider of energy for export purposes. It reinforces the notion that Canada's future is to be more and more a hewer of wood and a drawer of water with this increased dependence of our well being on the export of our natural resources instead of using our natural resources as a tool to attract investment to Canada and to create jobs at home rather than creating jobs abroad.
That notion has not penetrated the foggy collective minds of this cabinet. Probably they do not have one, or if they do it is so thick that they have not yet understood that energy means jobs and that if you insist on exporting energy and expanding those energies, you export jobs. Is that not elementary? We are facing a profound malaise

December 11, 1989
Government Orders
in the thoughts of this government as to what constitutes the long-term interest of Canadians when it comes to energy.
The fourth disturbing aspect in Bill C-23 is the total absence of any reference to the importance of renewable sources of energy as a mandate that the National Energy Board should not only make its own but also strengthen and expand. Obviously, one day we are going to run out of our non-renewable sources of energy. At least when it comes to oil, the horizons are already visible. With natural gas, perhaps they are beyond the horizon, we do not know. The same may be said of coal. But in the very long term we cannot hope and expect that these resources will remain forever available. They will run out.
Therefore, when you discuss a bill that relates to the National Energy Board, it is necessary to introduce as a responsibility the concept and the importance of giving renewable sources of energy the place that they deserve.
It is astonishing to learn from the minutes of the proceedings in committee that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources would say that the board may be perceived to be in an apparent conflict of interest situation and that "the board would literally be deciding how much more work it makes for itself", when it comes to the question of public hearings. I can hardly believe that a minister of the Crown would interpret the role of one of the major agencies under his or her jurisdiction in that manner, as an agency whose main task would be one of deciding how much more work it can create.
Obviously, if that is the opinion that the Minister of Energy has of the government's own National Energy Board, then a change is necessary at the top, namely a change with the minister himself.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-23 would seek to amend the National Energy Board Act if you take the bill literally at face value from its cover. That it is what it proclaims on the cover sheet.
If you read the bill in the form we have it to date, without the amendments that are being proposed, you will find that a more apt characterization of what Bill C-23 does is to gut the National Energy Board Act. So
that is why I rise in support of the first group of amendments put forward by my colleague for Malpeque.
If you were to listen to the rhetoric of this government, one of the themes that comes through again and again, whether you are talking about VIA Rail, Canada Post, or so many other Crown agencies, is that this government because of its basic purity of ideology maintains an arm's length relationship. That has been the message again and again. This government has repeatedly sent out the signal that its philosophy or way of operating is to give agencies statutory authority and let them operate within that authority to make decisions within their mandated area.
What is happening here in so far as the National Energy Board is concerned is that we have an agency with adequate statutory authority and broad powers that has ensured over the years that Canadians, both individually and in groups, can automatically through the vehicle of public hearing have their say whenever there is a contemplation to export electricity out of this country. Under statute there is a provision that there be a public hearing by the NEB.
Mr. Speaker, does it not make you back up and wonder what is behind the effort here to restrict the National Energy Board's ability to proceed with a public inquiry? As I pointed out, it flies in the face of the way in which this government has been operating on Canada Post and VIA Rail, just to use two examples.
In this case the government is going against the strain. It is going in the opposite direction. It is not arm's length-it is fingertip. The government wants to keep the question of electricity exports right at its fingertips. What does it provide in its unamended legislation? It provides that the cabinet will decide as to whether or not there will be a public inquiry.
I direct you to an example, Mr. Speaker. We all know how American Express got into this country in the way it did. We all know it was not as a result of any public inquiry. We all know that it was as a result of an order in council, a cabinet decision, made either on election day or hours before election day.


I submit to you, Sir, that the timing of that decision was no accident, that American Express' entry into Canada, and the fact that the decision was made on election day or thereabouts, was a direct trade-off between American Express' support for the government's position on free trade and American Express' objective of getting involved in the Canadian financial community.
By example that is my concern with this piece of legislation and that particular provision in it. It is that once again government gives to itself the vehicle, the wherewithal to do a political trade-off. It is not the NEB that will decide whether an inquiry is needed. Under this legislation the NEB will have to go to cabinet and ask it to make the decision.
Compare that procedure with what happens with the competition bureau, which is provided for in legislation introduced, sponsored by and passed by the current government. At the competition bureau the director of competition, up until recently Mr. Cal Goldman, makes the decision. He makes the determination as to whether or not there will be an inquiry-in the words of the act, a tribunal. It is left in that case to the judgment of a senior bureaucrat. I have difficulty with that because the discretion is left in the hands of one person. I raise it here in terms of an example to draw a contrast for you, Sir.
In the one case government has deemed that something as important as the merger of Canadian Airlines and Wardair, or the merger of Imperial and Texaco, to use a recent example and a very current one in the case of Imperial and Texaco, is to be left to the decision of one man, a bureaucrat. But on the question of exporting electricity, energy from this country is taken out of the hands of the National Energy Board which has administered it very competently over the years, and it is now put into political hands. I submit that it is being done for a very direct reason.
I come back to what my colleague from Davenport was saying when he spoke a few moments ago. He was asking whether this government has a mind or whether it has a collective mind. I would say to him: "Yes, this government has a mind all right."
