speechtext: It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 38, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: The hon. member for Brant-National Defence; the hon. member for Saskatoon-Clark's Crossing-Health; and the hon. member for Burnaby-Human Rights.

The House resumed consideration of Bill C-23, an Act to amend the National Energy Board Act and to repeal certain enactments in consequence thereof, as reported (with amendments) from a legislative committee; and the motion of Ms. Callbeck.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak to the amendment put forward by my colleague from Malpeque. The issue is the fact that the legislation as it now stands leaves a tremendous amount of not only power in the hands of cabinet itself but, as my colleague so ably pointed out a few minutes ago, power in the hands of one or two individuals who will be advising cabinet on these issues.
My colleague from Malpeque spoke very eloquently about the impact that this bill would have on the environment. I want to expand on that very briefly and speak about the environment in which we live in close proximity in many cases to high voltage transmission lines. I have a proposed line across the constituency of Lambton-Middlesex. I say "proposed" line because we already have two lines at the present time. They are
230,000	volt lines. One of them will be raised to 550,000 volts.
Until recently, until some of the citizens started to complain, they were going to take these right through the heart of three small villages and in close proximity to a fourth. Yet I do not see any guidelines in this legislation whereby cabinet would be directed to keep away from the built-up areas. There are enough questions at the present time to indicate that these transmission lines do impact on human health. In fact, if you are wearing a pacemaker you do not dare go anywhere close to a high voltage transmission line or else your pacemaker will act up and you could have very serious health problems resulting immediately.
I think we have to stop and examine the type of power we are leaving in the hands of the cabinet when there are no guidelines established at the present time regarding how close these lines can be to built-up areas. There are some areas in the United States where they make them stay back approximately 1,700 feet from a built-up area. In Russia it is 2,300 feet.
Yet when we talk about this here in Canada they say there is no proof that these lines do have an impact on human health. There is no proof that they do not have an impact on it either.
I think it is foolhardy for us to go through with a piece of legislation that does not recognize that there is an area here that must be studied further as to the impact on what it does to an individual. It is well documented as to what it will do to a dairy herd that is pasturing under one of these high voltage transmission lines, or a milking herd that is living in a yard or a bam close by. There are problems with conception in those herds. There are problems with the milking in that the quantity of milk produced drops dramatically.
In my constituency I have an individual who has a dog kennel close by one of these lines. He could not understand why the dogs killed their pups at birth if they did conceive. A lot of the dogs would not conceive until they took them a few kilometres away to another location. If there are impacts on the health of animals living in close proximity, then what is it going to do to humans who live close by?
There is a lot of suspicion at the present time that this may cause cancer, particularly to young people. I also have to point out that a young person in close proximity to one of these 230,000 volt transmission lines is already being treated for that dreaded disease at the present time.
We do not know enough about the electromagnetic fields that are created by these transmission lines. I suggest that it is not acceptable to Canadians to place the health of our citizens at risk in order to export energy to another country. It is fundamentally wrong to give such powers to cabinet to circumvent hearings whereby people are allowed to speak. It is morally wrong to allow any utility to create an environment that is dangerous to
December 11, 1989

public health for the sake of exporting power to another country and placing the health of our citizens at risk.
I suggest that to allow cabinet to bypass public hearings would deprive Canadians of the chance to voice their concerns they may have about the serious health consequences I spoke about. Before any decision like this is left to cabinet there have to be guidelines drafted based on information now available. If it is not available in Canada, then let us look at the records and the measures being used in other countries. We need guidelines that place the health of the citizens of this nation first and foremost.
I suggest that these guidelines should not be drafted by the utility companies but by known experts in the field who have watched the development of these transmission lines, not only in this nation but in the nation to the south of us, and Russia. This must be done recognizing that in many cases the utility companies are more interested in the export of power and the profits generated thereby than in the health of those who are living close by.
I would ask this House to support the amendment put forward by the member from Malpeque. I do so because of the unknowns that are facing us here and the tremendous amount of power that is to be left in the hands of cabinet to bypass these public hearings that give our citizens a chance to voice their concerns.
I recently attended a meeting in my constituency where one of these high voltage transmission lines was being discussed. There was a tremendous depth of fear there that was based on the best information available. The utility company downplayed it and tried to assure the people in attendance that there really was no problem. If there was a problem, it would tell them about it. The people did not accept that, and I do not accept it either. If that is the kind of information that is going to be available to the cabinet when it makes a decision to bypass the public hearings, then we as Canadian citizens deserve better. It is for that reason that I wholeheartedly support the amendment of my colleague from Malpeque.

She said: Mr. Speaker, this motion contains amendments which follow the ones in the previous motion. They deal basically with the same issues-cabinet powers, public hearings and the reputation of the National Energy Board. They also deal with the subject of interprovincial power lines.
I urge this House to adopt the motion for the same reasons that I stated earlier. It would eliminate the potential for unhelpful and potentially very harmful political interference by the federal cabinet.
It would do this by leaving the decision as to whether a public hearing on an application to the National Energy Board would be held not up to the cabinet but up to the board. I think the reasons stated during debate on the previous motion are well understood and need only summarizing here.
The fact is that when trusted to decide in the national interest in similar situations in the past the federal cabinet decided rather in its own political interest. We saw this with the Rafferty Dam in Saskatchewan, with James Bay, with VIA, and I suspect that we will see it under Bill C-23, unless these amendments are adopted.
We heard from a lot of witnesses before the legislative committee on Bill C-23. Some of them indicated that they feel this bill will not accomplish the goal of deregulation, but may in fact do just the opposite. That is to say that it may cause more headaches for the electric utilities than it solves.
With such a conflict between what government claims to be the purpose of the bill and what industry says it will accomplish, the real reason behind Bill C-23 becomes clear. That reason is simply to give the cabinet the power to control Canada's electricity trade to a far greater extent than it does today, and certainly more than is in the national interest.
Some of the most interesting testimony that we heard on Bill C-23 came from the minister himself. At our committee the minister gave a somewhat incredible explanation as to why cabinet wants more power over the National Energy Board. The minister says that the board may be perceived to be in an apparent conflict-of-interest situation because: "The board would literally be deciding how much more work it makes for itself".
As you know, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-23 will mean that the board will have decide whether to recommend to cabinet that an application before it go to a public inquiry, or whether adequate regulation is already in place.
I would like to draw to the attention of the minister the National Energy Board's reasons for a decision regarding Trans Mountain Pipeline of July, 1988. The length of this pipeline was such that the board did not have to hold a hearing. In its report the NEB decided to hold a public hearing on the application, thereby making more work for itself.
The government does not seem to have any problems with the NEB's powers on its potential for a conflict of interest when it comes to pipelines. For what reason should the government be taking this power away from the board and giving it to the cabinet when it comes to electricity exports and international power lines? I suggest that it is a purely political one. Certainly, the witnesses whom we had before the legislative committee hinted at this.
The witnesses we have heard have pretty well all expressed nothing but the highest faith in the board and its procedures, which means that they believe not only in the people who make up this board who are there now but in the whole process. Take for example the minister's parliamentary secretary who said he had full faith in the National Energy Board, in the guidelines and in the people who work within the board.
He also said he was certain that if they feel any of the guidelines are not met, any public hearings or input required will be there. This seems to contradict what the minister has said about the board not wanting to make more work for itself. I certainly have to agree with the comments of the parliamentary secretary as I have just quoted him. It seems that practically every witness that we had before this committee agreed.

The Quebec Cree have not had that much faith in the NEB, but they have even less faith in the federal cabinet. Really who can blame them?
New Brunswick Power is more complimentary and well represents the evidence given before the committee. I want to quote what it had to say: "The point is that after 30 years of operation the National Energy Board has not acted in a rogue way. It has acted in a highly respectable way. Its decisions have been a credit to the Government of Canada".
It seems that the only person who doubts the National Energy Board's character is the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. He has more faith, understandably, in his own cabinet whose opinions he knows and can count on. But not so the Cree who say: "We need an independent body which is concerned about the public, not a party that has gotten into power, not Progressive Conservatives, NDP or Liberals". I could not agree more.
Also in agreement with this last point is the advisory committee of the energy options report that this government set up in 1987. The committee states in its report:
It is of paramount importance that the NEB be seen as a
non-political institution if it is to ensure that its messages to
Canadians are effective and credible.
We agree. Therefore we are concerned that a board that gets overruled on major decisions often enough by cabinet may in time lose some of its credibility.
Just last month the committee's former chairman, Tom Kierans, told our committee that the board ought to be free to inquire into something and the inquiry ought to be public. He said that the only instance in which the cabinet should intervene is at the end of the process, after the NEB makes its final decision. Again, this is exactly our position. That is why we are proposing this motion.
Let me add one last piece of testimony on this point. It comes from the legal counsel to the Maritime Electric of Charlottetown who stated: "The NEB ought to be given authority to designate exports rather than authority only to recommend designation."
The evidence on this point is clear and it points in the direction of giving the National Energy Board the power to regulate in Canada's national interest. I have more arguments to make regarding Bill C-23 and these deal

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Buikley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to make a few brief comments on the second grouping of amendments to Bill C-23 which is before the House today. The member for Burin-St. George's commented about the concerns that we have on this side, and I trust and hope that members opposite also have, about the politicization of the National Energy Board. In fact, I think the government has made a mistake in the title of the bill. It should more accurately read, "an act to gut the National Energy Board and to unduly politicize the export of electricity from Canada" because for all intents and purposes that is exactly what Bill C-23 is doing in this legislation that we are debating
We are beginning to see the results of this government's record of making decisions within cabinet, behind the curtains, behind closed doors where the public does not have an opportunity to participate, to discuss, or to share in those decisions. The decision regarding VIA Rail has already been mentioned today, the complete about face by the government from its previous position when the Liberals were cutting VIA Rail. We now have the example of the Conservatives in office cutting VIA Rail with no public hearings or any other provisions. If the Canadian public asks for anything when government is making decisions on such critical issues as hydroelectric lines or the export of power, it is that those decisions are made with ample opportunity for public input. In many cases, all we ask for is a chance to make our comments then, fair enough, a decision has to be made at some point.
Bill C-23, which we are debating today, goes in completely the opposite direction of the kind of openness that all members of this House have been calling for, at least certainly those on this side of the chamber. I know that my colleague, the member for Edmonton East, raised these matters in committee in the legislative review of this bill. We are rising here today in support of the Liberal amendments because we think they will help move this legislation in the right direction. I certainly call

Government Orders
on the government members also to support this very important amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I would also like to speak to these motions, especially the motions proposed by my colleague for Malpeque.
Bill C-23 is really a wolf in sheep's clothing or vice versa. I am very worried about some of the things that are being proposed today. One of them is the politicizing of the decisions on our future energy needs and of the power lines. In effect, this bill states that the National Energy Board can now recommend a public hearing and the cabinet will decide whether they will agree or disagree with the National Energy Board.
A comment that I have heard is that of course the cabinet is always going to act in the highest regard because there is always public pressure. I hasten to point out to some members opposite that that is not always the case with this cabinet, sometimes, there are other times when political expediency certainly plays a very large role in their decisions. I will bring to light something that came up just recently, and that was a request by the Auditor General that the cabinet release documents concerning their travel expenditures. The cabinet decided not to release these documents because it was not necessary, or for whatever reason they had, but I do not believe this decision is in the public interest. It would be far more in the public interest to have the details released.
What happens if the National Energy Board decides that there should be a public hearing because the provinces concerned have not held the proper hearings and the cabinet decides not to? There is nothing preventing the cabinet from deciding against a public hearing.
Future energy needs and the whole reason for the National Energy Board would be undone. Because cabinet can overrule any decision, why even bother with a National Energy Board, if that is the case? I believe that the future energy needs of our country have to be safeguarded. They must be safeguarded. One must not play lightly with some of the best resources that we have here in our country, and that is our energy.
With these amendments the National Energy Board would have the power to ask for a hearing and I believe it should have this power. Therefore, I support the amendments of my colleague.

She said: Mr. Speaker, these motions deal with many important issues raised by Bill C-23. They include free trade, the environment, and the whole question about how clear this legislation could be.
The last point is certainly important because Parliament has an obligation to make its laws as clear as possible so that misunderstandings do not arise.
First, the issue of free trade. The motion before the House would make Canada's electricity exports to the U.S. with regard to Article 904 of the free trade agreement an explicit concern of the National Energy Board. As the House knows, Canada exports a great deal of electricity to the United States, but with the free trade
Government Orders
agreement Canada has to guarantee the Americans an opportunity to buy these exports in the future.
Generally speaking, if Canada is forced to cut back on exports for some reason, we have to guarantee the United States the chance to bid on the same proportion of exports we sent them during the previous three years. The other side of the arrangement is that we can only cut the supply to the Americans if we do the same to Canadians. Therefore, we along with other groups, feel that it is a good idea that the National Energy Board be given responsibility for making sure that Canada does not bite off more than it can chew. That is, we want to ensure that Canada can sustain its level of exports for some time so that Article 904 of the free trade agreement does not come crashing down on us.
The Council of Canadians has certainly supported this idea. It recommended to our standing committee the widening of the mandate of the NEB to take into account the new situation under the free trade agreement with the proportionality clause. The government may scoff at the advice of the Council of Canadians, which opposed the trade deal during the election last year, but the same argument was also made by the advisory committee to the Energy Options Report which this government set up in 1987. This report advocates a market based approach on most energy matters, but on one issue they are clearly in favour of involvement by the NEB, and that one issue is free trade.
The committees say in the Energy Options Report that with free trade it becomes even more important to keep a vigilant watch over export levels to ensure that they do not exceed long-term sustainable proportions. That is exactly what this motion will accomplish.
The government has said that there are issues and matters today which were not foreseeable when the NEB act was originally passed in 1959. Surely concern about the environment is one of those issues, and some duplication of provincial regulations may be a second. But there can be no doubt that a major new development is the free trade agreement which will be colouring Canada's energy policy for many years to come.
What happens when one province's exports of electricity significantly tilt the balance for all of Canada? All of Canada will have the responsibility of meeting our export requirements under Section 904 of the free trade agree-

December 11, 1989
Government Orders
ment. With responsibility come certain rights. In this instance, all of Canada through the National Energy Board should have a right to examine this country's energy exposure to the United States.
This motion will also ensure that the National Energy Board considers how an export affects Canada's energy supply position. The government says that the question of surplus is not as important today as it was back in 1959 when Prime Minister Diefenbaker said the NEB was supposed to ensure that exports were: "surplus to the needs of the Canadian economy in this and foreseeable generations in order to ensure for Canadians an adequate supply of the natural resources which are the heritage of this country-"
We are told that provincial utilities will only export when they are in a surplus position. But will this always be the case? A recent article in The Globe and Mail reports that demand is threatening to outstrip supply for the first time in Hydro Quebec's history. The crunch is the result of low water levels in the James Bay area and also labour difficulties at Hydro Quebec. Hydro Quebec says that no one could have foreseen today's climate conditions. But that is not the point. The point is that if utilities are not going to plan in case of shortages, someone should. We think that someone should be the National Energy Board.
This motion also contains an amendment that aims to further protect the environment from the effects of electricity projects. The goal here is to allow a preliminary study of an application that is presented to the NEB. There would be a preliminary study Office, and that study would help the National Energy Board decide whether to hold a full public hearing on the application. FEARO would report its decision to the National Energy Board and they would make that recommendation public. The advantages of this is that FEARO is an independent body. It is free from political interference. The Minister of the Environment cannot tell it what to do. The minister, however, must be responsible to Parliament for FEARO's work and can be questioned on such matters in the House.
For these many reasons, I recommend that the House adopt this motion. This motion also deals with some small matters which were raised in committee. Some confusion exists as to whether the National Energy Board can act in the public interest where the province being examined takes no action to be complemented by
the National Energy Board. The original bill said that the board could complement measures taken by the provinces of regulating electricity, but what happens when provinces take no action of their own? As Maritime Electric has stated, you cannot complement measures-add to something-if they have not been taken in the first place. So, if no provincial measures get taken, there will be no measures for the National Energy Board to complement.
While the government amended the bill in committee to take out the words "complement measures", we would still like to amend it in this way, because for one thing the wording of our amendment accomplishes several things, this technical correction being only one. In the interests of efficiency, this amendment is still being proposed.
Some confusion also exists as to which province the board ought to look at. Should it be the province where the electricity is generated or the province from which the electricity leaves Canada, or both, or even three provinces may be involved once in a while. This change means that the board can look at measures taken or not taken in whatever province it finds relevant. Again, as Maritime Electric told us, even if Parliament expresses itself clearly, differences in interpretation of legislation will occur. That means if Parliament does not express itself clearly, differences and disputes are almost certain to arise.
For all the reasons stated above, I urge the House to adopt this third motion.

Mr. Speaker, I rise again to speak on the third grouping of amendments to Bill C-23, the act to gut the National Energy Board and unduly politicize electricity exports, and to make a few comments before our hour of adjournment.
We on this side of the House have already expressed concern about the independence of the National Energy Board, or how it is threatened by this legislation, because it is going to allow cabinet to overrule the NEB on energy projects and power lines. The same point has to be made in relation to electricity exports. The energy future of Canada demands that our consideration of proposals for the export of electricity continues to be characterized by impartiality and prudence. By allowing cabinet to override the NEB in order to increase exports,
December 11, 1989

this bill politicizes that process and thereby threatens the national interest.
As I mentioned earlier, my colleague for Edmonton East, our energy critic, made this point on many occasions in committee. Unfortunately the government did not see fit to adopt some of the amendments that he proposed. We rise today to support the amendments presented by the member for Malpeque. They appear to be not necessarily aimed specifically at the problem, but do happen to have the effect of helping to maintain the independence of the NEB and we support that.
My colleagues and I pointed out during debate at second reading of this bill that the government was putting in place a mechanism that would make public hearings on export proposals very rare. In fact, under this bill the granting of export permits will be routine and public hearings for the vast majority of export applications will not be held. We pointed that there was no good evidence that the existing process was overly burdensome. In fact, evidence at the committee hearings show that this was the case. We pointed out that a closed process seldom serves the public purpose well. We have heard other examples of that today, VIA Rail being one, especially when dealing with such an important strategic resource like electricity. Once again, my colleague proposed in committee that a public hearing on major export proposals be held by someone at either the provincial or the federal level. This very sensible suggestion was turned down.
The main focus of this set of amendments, the third grouping, is to allow the NEB to refer proposals to export electricity to the Federal Environmental Assessment Review Office. We understand that the spirit of the Brundtland Commission demands that the effect of public policy on the environment should be considered in all sectors of government. That means all departments and all agencies of government. It means that the NEB itself will be charged with conducting the basic environmental assessments of its decisions. Bill C-23 makes some progress in that regard. Under the proposal envisioned in this amendment, FEARO, the Environmental Assessment Review Office would be used as the "environmental protector of last resort to make assessments of those export proposals the NEB feels that it cannot handle adequately itself." That sounds like an entirely
Government Orders
sensible idea and something that the prudent member for Edmonton East would recommend.
Let us take a look at how some of these amendments affect the most important free trade agreement as it now impacts between our country and the United States. My colleague, the energy critic, the member for Edmonton East, pursued this bill in some detail when it was in committee, and he offered a number of amendments. In effect, by signing the energy provisions of the free trade deal, the government has placed a boa constrictor around our neck. Under the trade deal, exports of energy to the United States will never decrease in relative terms, but will much more likely increase and increase. Article 904 of the FTA states:
Either Party may maintain or introduce a restriction-with respect to the export of an energy good-only if:
a) the restriction does not reduce the proportion of the total export shipments of a specific energy good made available to the other Party relative to the total supply of that good of the Party maintaining the restriction compared to the proportion prevailing in the most recent 36-month period -
Now that makes a lot of sense. This proportionality clause is like a ratchet that gets tighter and tighter. It is like a boa constricter, squeezing its prey and it never lets up. That is why it is so dangerous for Canada's energy future.
The point that has been missed in all of this, when it comes to electricity exports, a kilowatt hour is a kilowatt hour is a kilowatt hour. A buck is a buck is a buck. It does not matter if an export consists of a long-term firm contract or merely supplies of interruptable power, every kilowatt hour of power that we export defines the amount that we must offer the United States in following years. It will not be a one-off deal. If that amount is more than we usually send, the ratchet, that boa con-stricter will tighten. The proportion that we will have to offer the U.S. will continue to increase and we will have lost forever that degree of energy flexibility that we talked about so proudly before in this House.
We know that this government, this party delivered the free trade deal for its friends in big business. We know that they are not even proud enough to tell us where their donations were from. Members in this House have

Private Members' Business
to do that. I only expect that from those people who bought all of those ads during the election campaign.
In the meantime, the least we can do is ensure that the National Energy Board takes the ratchet effect, that boa constricter again, into account in every one of its decisions respecting electricity exports. That is prudent. It is simple common sense. It is something we hope this government will follow.

The House resumed from Tuesday, October 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. Althouse:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of introducing measures to amend the Western Grain Stabilization Act to include coverage for producers who feed their own grain to their livestock; and on the amendment of Mr. Funk:
That the motion be amended by adding immediately after the words "Western Grain Stabilization Act" the following:
'and Agricultural Stabilization Act'.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to continue my speech on this motion and the record of safety net programs such as the Western Grain Stabilization Program and the Agricultural Stabilization Program.
In recent years, world grain subsidy battles, heavy debt loads and drought have combined to place Canada's grains industry under tremendous pressure. Changes in the world trade environment have led to a re-examination of the role of government support programs. Many of us from this House have joined hundreds of producers and others concerned in the agricultural industry at the minister's agri-food conference today at the Congress Centre. They are there to initiate the most thorough review of agriculture undertaken in this country for many years. Government support programs are going to be part of that review.
Programs like the Western Grain Stabilization Act and the Agriculture Stabilization Act have been doing the job that they were designed to do, protecting producers from the impact of a sudden drop in cash flow because of disruptions in markets or production costs.
The WGSA was set up in 1976 to stabilize farm incomes when grain prices dropped below a five-year average. The program has done just that. Since the 1985-86 crop year the Western Grain Stabilization Act has paid out over $3.2 billion to participants in the Prairie provinces.

A farmer who had been enrolled since the beginning of the program will have received $6 in benefit payments for every dollar of levy contributed. Over the same period the Agricultural Stabilization Act has also made substantial payments to grain and oilseed producers in eastern Canada and to producers whose products are not included under the Western Grain Stabilization Program. These programs are working but that does not mean that they cannot be improved.
Since 1984 the government has been working with producers and their organizations to make the Western Grain Stabilization Act more responsive to the needs of those producers.
In February of 1985, the Western Grain Stabilization Act was amended so that in years when a substantial pay-out was evident, interim payments would be made before the end of the crop year. This provided farmers with cash when they needed it most in time for spring seeding.
The program was further improved in 1988. Amendments were made to encourage participation, extend crop coverage and put the program on a sound financial footing. A10 per cent penalty for producers rejoining the program was removed, and the deadline for non-participating producers to join the Western Grain Stabilization Act was extended.
Nine additional crops were made eligible for payments. These included buckwheat, peas, lentils, fab-abeans, canary seed, mixed grain, sunflower and safflower seeds.
Amendments were also passed to raise levies in the joint government-producer funded program. The federal government now pays 6 per cent, instead of 3 per cent, of eligible grain sale receipts while producer levies increased from 1 per cent to 4 per cent. This combined with a write-down of $750 million of the stabilization fund deficit put the program on a sounder financial basis. Without this write-down, the future of the program was in doubt.
The 1988 amendments provided immediate benefits to producers for the 1987-88 crop year. Producers rejoining the program received about 70 per cent of the payment that a full participant with the same level of grain sales received. The payment level increased to 85 per cent for the 1988-89 crop year. Without the amendments, producers rejoining the program would have received only 30 per cent of the full payment.
Private Members' Business
The success of these improvements is in the statistics. Participation has increased 8 per cent since the latest amendments, to the highest level since the program began. It now stands at 90 per cent of eligible Wheat Board permit book holders. The total number of participating producers is over 129,000, up from 113,000 in the 1986-87 crop year, an increase of 12 per cent.
This government is willing to consider further amendments to improve safety net programs for farmers. Today, we are being asked to consider the inclusion of farm-fed grain in the Western Grain Stabilization Program.
The issue is not new. The present program provides protection to farmers based on grain sales receipts. However, it does not cover farm-fed grain. Producers who feed a large portion of the grain they grow to livestock are not included.
Since this issue and motion was first discussed in the House, I had the occasion to discuss it with a number of my farmers. Many of these people would benefit from the program if it were extended. They asked me point blank why I was not promoting and actively supporting this. I have assured them that the government is taking a very broad look at the issue. The farm sector clearly needs assistance to improve its long term financial stability.
In recent years we have relied on ad hoc government support programs such as the 1986 and 1987 Special Canadian Grains Program, which paid out $2.1 billion to producers, and the 1988 Canadian Crop Drought Assistance Program, which paid producers another $850 million. But designing a special program for each crisis situation is not the answer.
Farmers also agree that whatever we do must be consistent with international efforts to reform agricultural subsidies.
Last April in Geneva ministers from countries involved in talks under GATT agreed that the long term objective of the negotiations is to establish a fair and market oriented agricultural trading system. The short term agreement provides that current support and protection levels in the agricultural sector will not be increased during the period of the negotiations. Countries have agreed not to change policies in a manner which would further restrict access to markets.

December 11, 1989
Private Members' Business
The government is now involved in an extensive review of Canadian agricultural policies. The review was launched in the summer of 1988 and grain stabilization is part of that total review. Government representatives met with farm leaders across the country to determine options for a national stabilization program. These options were developed by Agriculture Canada's National Grains Bureau in Winnipeg and presented to a meeting of farm leaders. Discussions have continued and right now a national conference discussing policy directions for the future is under way at the Congress Centre.
The issue of farm-fed grain will likely be raised at that conference but will be examined in the light of a need for a stabilization program, but one which treats Canadian farmers in an equitable way.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to say a few words on Motion No. 310 which requests the government to consider doing something about the effect of paying stabilization on grain that is sold commercially but not paying stabilization on farm fed grain.
At present most people involved in the production of grain recognize that the terms of the Western Grain Stabilization Act and the Agricultural Stabilization Act do not treat those who produce the grain and sell it on the commercial market in the same way as those farmers who grow the grain and then feed it to their own livestock. The process is very clear.
I was reviewing the remarks made by the member from Brandon-Souris and wondered why the government is being somewhat dense on this in the sense that it does not seem to recognize that there is a detrimental effect upon the rural communities because of the forced separation, to a great extent, of the meat sector in farming from that of the grain producing sector.
The Stabilization Act kicks in when farmers growing and selling their grain on the commercial market get a low market price. Otherwise stabilization acts would not become effective. The stabilization payment they get brings them somewhat closer to the cost of production.
The farmer who grows that grain and feeds it to his own livestock does not get that stabilization payment. Even if he is on the stabilization for one of the hog programs or one of the beef programs, the cost of that
cheap grain is factored in. In other words, the stabilization payment is lost to that particular farmer. He does not get it as part of his income for that year.
This has had the effect of forcing families to separate their feeding operations from their growing operations to the point where, in some cases, they quit one of them entirely and sell the grain to the neighbour when, if farm-fed grains were treated the same way as commercial grains as far as stabilization was concerned, those farmers would continue to produce cattle and hogs.
The Pork Marketing Council makes a very good case. It suggests that this different treatment of people who grow their grain and feed it to their livestock and those who sell it on the commercial market is so detrimental that it is forcing some farmers to leave the production of hogs and go entirely into the production of grain in those years when make veiy much money producing either the feed or the hogs. Consequently, the need for the stabilization becomes very obvious.
This Motion No. 310 asks the government to deal with this discrimination in some way. It does not suggest that we eliminate either one or the other of the programs. It suggests that in the process of dealing with this, one has to look at the differentiation, recognize that there is a differentiation and then do something about it.
That was the recommendation made to the Department of Agriculture by Daryl Kraft a number of years ago. And it is the recommendation made by a good number of farm organizations which have had the opportunity to make presentations to the government. Daiyl Kraft included the recommendation, when he made his report, that farm-fed grains be made eligible for stabilization coverage. He gave two alternatives that the government could consider in order to close that gap. The government has taken no action on this recommendation at all.
The pork producers go on to suggest that there should be no difference in the treatment of grain that is fed to the livestock operation on the same farm on which it is is grown and grains sold through commercial channels. If there were no difference between the two, we would not have the situation that is negatively affecting rural

communities with mixed farms that have small numbers of livestock. Rather, farmers would specialize.
Not so long ago, a lot of our policies were established with the idea of getting people to produce more grain or more hogs. Now, under the present circumstances of the economy of agriculture, we need to take a look at those things and make sure that one of the programs does not detrimentally affect another, and that is all that is being asked here in Motion No. 310.

Mr. Speaker, I take pleasure in entering into this debate today. I might say to the hon. member who introduced the motion that it is not a motion void of merit. Certainly, it is one that commands our attention and reflection. And for those of us who live in agricultural communities, it is a fact that this motion is very much on the minds of those who are involved in a combination of both feeding and raising grains. The important point to underscore at the moment, however, is one that I am sure the hon. member for Mackenzie will appreciate. We have in Ottawa at the moment one of the largest collections of farm leaders from across Canada who are disposed in part with this very question.
Because they are undertaking to look at and review the nature of feeding farm grains and the relationship that ought to be with the whole question of grain support programs, it would seem to me that it would be an important consideration to wait until they have had the opportunity, as farm leaders, to reflect upon this matter. They can give us the value and the wisdom of their good counsel before we, as members, make a precipitous motion that might put us into a position which subsequently might lock us on to a direction for which the farm community itself might want to go with some variance or in some slightly different direction.
The Western Grain Stabilization Program and the Agricultural Stabilization Programs provide supports to producers when grain prices drop below the five-year average. However, livestock producers in both eastern and western Canada have expressed concern that farm-fed grain is not included in the two stabilization programs. In some livestock support programs the price of grain is included in the formula for triggering these programs. So, when grain prices rise, support prices for
Private Members' Business
livestock rise. But livestock support programs do not account for the cost of producing farm-fed grain. If the price of grain is unchanged but grain production costs increase, this is not reflected in the payments through livestock support programs.
This is an important issue but it should not be considered in isolation. Including farm-fed grain in stabilization programs is an issue which must be looked at in the broad context of all agricultural stabilization programs. Including farm-fed grain in the Western Grain Stabilization Act and the ASA seems like a simple way to provide additional protection to producers who feed grain to their livestock. It really is not. Including farm-fed grain in these programs would create a whole new set of issues.
First, some stabilization programs, such as the dairy program, already include a portion of the cost of producing farm-fed grains. If farm-fed grains were included in the Western Grain Stabilization and the ASA some producers would receive compensation twice on the same grain. Second, including farm-fed grain in the Western Grain Stabilization and the ASA would change these programs completely. Both programs would be based on production rather than on commercial sales. This has a number of implications. Both the Western Grain Stabilization Act and the ASA were based on production. Good yield data would be essential. Individual yield data would likely not be available in all cases and the program would have to be administered on the basis of regional yield averages.
Farmers will not be getting payments based on individual data and that could raise some questions of inequity. Producers with yields below the regional average would be overpaid and those with higher yields would, unfortunately, be underpaid.
Including farm-fed grain in the Western Grain Stabilization Act and the ASA may give livestock producers more protection. But taking this step would remove the protection which the grain producers have from being unable to market their grain.
Right now if producers cannot make deliveries, that is reflected in the reduced sales and the Western Grain Stabilization Act payment can be triggered. If the West-

December 11, 1989
Private Members' Business
em Grain Stabilization Act were based on production, payments under both programs would not be triggered because of reduced deliveries.
Finally, including farm-fed grain in the Western Grain Stabilization Act and the ASA, would make both programs more expensive. In the case of the Western Grain Stabilization Act, farmers would share those increased costs along with the government.
Farm-fed grain plays a significant role in our agricultural economy. About half of the cereal crops produced in Canada, excluding wheat, are fed to livestock. In the Maritimes, the proportion of farm-fed grain is even higher. Even when wheat is included, about 30 per cent of cereal crops are fed on farms. The federal government realizes the significance of farm-fed grain in our agricultural economy. We have talked with producers and their organizations about including farm-fed grain in the stabilization programs.
Most recently, in the summer of 1988, this issue was raised at a series of regional meetings with the Minister of Grains and Oilseeds held with farm organizations to discuss farm safety nets. Farm-fed grain was an issue raised at all of those meetings and it is an issue that was raised again in January, 1989 on farm safety nets held in Winnipeg.
The Standing Committee on Agriculture also looked into the issue of farm-fed grain in its January, 1986 report on the Western Grain Stabilization Act. This is what the committee concluded on the issue of farm-fed grain.
It should be only for the final products marketed that the producer receives market risk protection under the Western Grain Stabilization Act, or the ASA. In the case of livestock producers, they face the livestock market, but not the grain market risks. Treating livestock producers as grain producers means that the grain may be covered in the raw form and again as it goes into the final product.
That, I hasten to mention, was a recommendation of an all-party committee of this Parliament.
The federal government is about to undertake an agricultural policy review. One of the topics we will be discussing with producers and their organizations is how farm-fed grain should be dealt with under the grain income stabilization program. A number of suggestions have already been put forward for discussion. We have been debating just one of those options, including farm-fed grain in grain income stabilization programs.
Another option is including the cost of grain production in the formulas for calculating support under meat and poultry stabilization programs. This type of system is already in place for the dairy program. One drawback to this option is that livestock support prices would go up when the cost of grain production goes up, but not when actual grain prices rise. This would mean less protection for producers who buy feed rather than grow it themselves.
Another option is a program which would stabilize income for both livestock and grains. This option would be targeted toward the profitability of the producer's over-all operation. Livestock and grain incomes would not be considered then in isolation. The program would have to be operated at individual farm levels to take into account how significant livestock and grain receipts are to each operation.
The federal government is currently undertaking a review of all farm safety-net programs and the issue of farm-fed grain will be included in that policy review. The goal of the policy review is to work with industry and with the producers to knock out a national policy for Canadian agriculture.
The Minister of Agriculture has set out four principles as the basis for a national agricultural policy. They include market responses, self-reliance, sustainable and regional sensitivity. I would like to address the issue of market responsiveness and how it relates to the Western Grain Stabilization Act-

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the House for giving me an extension of time. I appreciate it very much.
I would like to address the issue of market responsiveness and how it relates to the Western Grain Stabilizatin Act and the ASA for a moment. Concern has been expressed that the two programs discourage the use of grain on farms as feed, and promote off-farm sales instead. The livestock sector represents a major opportu-

nity for value-added and diversification in the agriculture sector.
Here is what "The Road Not Taken", a study done by producers through the National Grains Bureau, "Grains 2000"program states about the opportunities for value-added activities in the meat sector:
The livestock sector serves as the principal feed stock to an expanded food processing sector. The meat processing sector represents the third largest industry in Canada with annual sales exceeding $8 billion. It employs 31,000 people with a payroll of $764 million and purchases almost $7 billion worth of goods and services a year. More importantly, it is almost totally a value-added industry. Properly managed, it could provide the main engine to a much more diversified and substantially better stabilized Canadian agriculture.
We are willing to work with industry to develop programs which will encourage value-added activities and diversification. But simply tinkering with the Western Grain Stabilization Act or the ASA will not be enough.
As I have pointed out, including farm-fed grains in these programs would bring a new set of inequities. We have to take a much more comprehensive approach. That is why the federal government is reviewing all agricultural programs, including the Western Grain Stabilization Act and the ASA. We want to find out how these programs affect market signals, the decisions producers make about their operations, the environment and the region, and we will be working with industry to come up with better policies and programs which will be more in tune with the needs of the industry.
With that, again, Mr. Speaker, I extend my appreciation to the House for the extended time that was allowed me to complete those comments.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate today, a debate about the extension of the Western Grain Stabilization program to the livestock producers who grow their own grain, as well as the amendment that extends the coverage under the Agriculture Stabilization Act to those same producers in other parts of the country.
I have to commend my colleague for bringing in a motion like this because I think it is time well spent, not only to look at the current issues but in consideration of the projected farm income figures for the coming year. We find that the incomes are going to be dropping drastically. In Ontario, incomes will be down by 8 per cent; in Manitoba, 87 per cent; in Alberta, 54 per cent,
Private Members' Business
and in Saskatchewan by 101 per cent. While these incomes to the producers are dropping like this, we see in the documents prepared for the conference today and in the news release they expect that pork prices will decline moderately in the next year even though beef prices may go up slightly.
Because we have the supply management systems in place for both dairy and poultry, they are not going to be hit as hard unless the government continues on its trend to pull away the underpinnings of these national supply marketing systems. Then, of course, there will be a return to the law of the jungle, disaster for all those involved and a massive take-over of those markets by the huge corporate farms to the south of us.
When you stop and look at the rationale behind the motion, you have to realize that those producers who grow their own grain always hit the same cycle. When the prices of grain are low, the livestock prices are similarly low as well. Even though they may qualify for tripartite stabilization on the livestock they are producing, at the same time that is only a break-even price and they have already suffered the same production losses. Those are the losses in their cost of production per acre on the grains they used to raise that livestock.
I am very concerned as I speak today because we have already seen many of our farm programs changed in the way of legislation. Most recently was the change in the Crop Insurance Act for the producer to be required to pay a full 50 per cent. Yet the federal government is going to get off the hook for 25 per cent of what the costs have been to it in the past, even though the provinces will be expected to pick up part of the balance of the costs.
I think it would have been much more prudent on behalf of the federal government when we have the forecast losses in the coming year to have put forward a bill that would have brought about a system of tripartite crop insurance.
I also have to think back on Bill C-36, the farm crop cash advances with the interest-free loans and how the government delayed from late in April when the budget was brought down until legislation was finally introduced in Parliament some five months later. Then it was brought through the House of Commons at second reading and into committee and out again. Then there

December 11, 1989
Private Members' Business
was a further delay of three weeks before it finally got third reading.
Also, we have to look at the At and East program that will impact dramatically on those in Atlantic Canada and on the availability of grain to them at reasonable prices. That is being removed at the present time under proposed legislation. I have to remind the government that this was an initial market for western grain that could now very well be filled by offshore grains and deprive our Canadian farmers in western Canada of yet another good market.
When I look at these various programs that are being phased out by this government, I wonder where all these ideas are coming from. Certainly they are not all cost cutting in terms of savings they are going to give to us. When we rob Peter to pay Paul, Canadians are still going to suffer.
In terms of farm crop cash advances, as I indicated when I spoke in that debate, the increase in taxes from tobacco and alcoholic beverages alone amounted to approximately $475 million in the last budget. Yet this total program only cost $27 million in terms of the crop advances. The rationale does not hold up that they are cutting some programs in an effort to control the deficit when, in fact, they raised the taxes on the same commodities that benefit from those programs by $475 million.
I have to reflect back to a speech made in the Senate committee on agriculture in Washington on April 19, 1989, a statement by Clayton Yeutter, the Secretary of Agriculture. At the top of page 7 he states that if the GATT negotiations are successful, we will be writing a segment of the European Community's 1991 farm bill in Geneva rather than in Brussels.
The Secretary of Agriculture in the United States is going to write the farm bills for these other countries in Europe. He goes on to state that this is obviously one of our objectives. Then he says that the U.S. will also be writing a major segment of the farm bills of Canada, Brazil, Argentina, Australia and several other countries in Geneva.
Here we have a U.S. Secretary of Agriculture writing farm bills for Canada. We see the proof of the pudding when we see these programs cancelled in the budget that came down in the House of Commons in the last few days of April, a leaked budget, I should add. Then we see
these programs brought in to be gutted or cancelled in the House of Commons.
I think it is deplorable that any nation such as this should have to dance to the tune played by a fiddler in Washington who openly admits he is going to write the farm policies for this country when a policy is desperately needed to provide more help to the farmers in Canada.
I received a letter from the Canadian Pork Council dated December 7, 1989, asking us to support this bill because it is desperately needed. Many of the pork producers grow their own grains but they too have been hit hard, not only by the disastrously low grain prices we have had since this Tory government came to power but also the fact that we have had three drought years. Particularly in my area, there have been droughts in 1985, 1987 and 1988.
I look at what has happened in western Canada, particularly in the province of Saskatchewan. Some areas of that province were hit equally hard this year as they were in the previous two years. Now is not the time to be cancelling some of these programs but rather it is the time to be adding to and broadening that support we have had in the past to cover the grain fed to livestock.
It is a sad commentary when I look at what is happening across this nation, particularly at a time just before Christmas when we have heard a lot of talk here about how many people have become unemployed during the last few weeks as the various plants laid off workers or announced closures. It is equally sad to see the plight of some of the farm people across this nation in the provinces. I am referring particularly to Saskatchewan. One man who called me this morning suggested that there would be as many as 8,000 farmers forced off their land this winter in Saskatchewan.
I call upon the government at this point to stop and take a look at what it is doing.
Eight thousand?

Up to 8,000. Those are the figures he gave me. I am not talking about Farm Credit Corporation, I am talking about the whole group regardless of where they are financed. There could be up to 8,000 forced off their land in Saskatchewan this winter. I heard that from a reasonably good authority, perhaps someone closer to it than a lot of members in this House. He is
December 11, 1989

involved with some church groups that are trying to find a way to help these people.
I think it is tragic that we find ourselves in a situation like this at this time of year before the Christmas season. It is tragic that we find ourselves in a situation where a province that is noted as being the bread-basket of the world is now forced into a position where its farmers cannot even make a break-even living, where they have to find outside employment, not only for the husband but for the wife, in order to carry on their operation.
This area has been neglected too long and I would have to suggest to this government that it is by the strengthening and building on the programs that are already there, rather than taking them away, that this problem will be resolved. It is with proposals such as the one we have here today that we will be able to maintain a strong livestock sector across this nation, rather than see the decline we have had in the last few years and the hardships inflicted upon these people.
I wholeheartedly support the proposal that is before the House this afternoon. I hope it will move forward for consideration into committee.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to participate in the debate on Motion No. 310 standing in the name of the member for Mackenzie, and its amendment.
I am tempted to address some of the comments made by the previous speaker, the member for Lambton- Middlesex, but I will resist that temptation and restrict my comments to the motion before us.
Motion No. 310 supports the inclusion of farm-fed grain into the existing stabilization programs for marketed grain. Including farm-fed grain in the grain stabilization framework is an issue we have heard brought up before by producers. It has been raised many times in previous years. In particular, the Prairie Pools, for example, have made the proposal recently.
The Western Grain Stabilization Program and the Agricultural Stabilization Act provide protection to farmers based on grain marketings. Farmers who do not market their grain, but instead feed it on their own farms
Private Members' Business
to livestock have argued that they need similar protection.
About half of the cereals other than wheat grown in Canada are fed to livestock on farms where the grain was grown. This is the case across most of the country, except in the maritimes where the proportion of farm-fed grain is higher. If we include wheat, about 30 per cent of the grain is fed on the farm.
Producers in western Canada feed slightly less of their grain production to livestock than is the case in eastern Canada. Amending either the WGSA or the ASA to include farm-fed grain would involve major changes in the structures of these programs. It would involve basing the calculations used to determine support levels on grain production instead of on grain sales.
A production-based program would rely on good yield data which may be very difficult to get. Using yield averages for different regions could penalize producers with higher yields while benefiting those with lower yields.
As we can see, the issue is a very complicated one. If changes are made to those programs, the result could well be stabilization programs which create more inequities than presently exist among regions and types of farm operations.
In addition, we can see this issue as one which involves producers in all regions. One of the earlier speakers, the member for Crowfoot, mentioned the 1986 report of the agriculture committee, and without mentioning some of the specifics that he mentioned, I would mention recommendation No. 10 of the committee in 1986. It was that undesignated sales remain ineligible under the Western Grain Stabilization Act. The two major reasons for this were that first of all it would be very difficult administratively because levy collection in the case of undocumented sales would create extreme difficulties and the second major reason was that the Western Grain Stabilization protection should only be for the final products marketed. In this case, the final product is the beef or hog production as the case may be.
Some protection for farm-fed grain does exist in the form of livestock support programs, but for the most part, those programs use market price for grain in support calculations rather than the cost of producing the grain. When grain prices fall, livestock support prices fall. For the producer who buys grain to feed his livestock, lower support prices reflect lower costs, but for

December 11, 1989
Private Members' Business
the producer who grows his own grain to use as feed, there is no reduction in costs to offset the reduced support price.
However, some dairy producers are at least partially protected as the cost of grain production is factored into the price support formula. To include the cost of producing grain into the price support calculations for all livestock programs would cause the reverse of the situation I have just explained. That is, when the costs of producing grain increase, the livestock support prices will increase. That is fair for the producer who grows his own feed, but protection is reduced for the farmer who has to buy his feed.
There are still inequities. This clearly indicates the importance of dealing with stabilization in a broader context. We must consider the impact that making changes to any stabilization program will have on other programs or other sectors of the industry.
This is why grain stabilization is a major component in the agricultural policy review now under way by the federal government. This comprehensive review is being undertaken to prepare Canada's agricultural industry to keep pace with the changing and increasingly globalized market-place. Our agriculture industry must be prepared for the next century, and a solid foundation for agriculture must be built now.
One of the more important considerations in this extensive review is the issue of safety nets. This is very timely because tomorrow morning, in fact, as part of the conference entitled "Growing Together", the agri-food conference being held in Ottawa this week, there is a major session on safety nets. This session is being chaired jointly by the Ministers of Agriculture for Manitoba and Newfoundland.
The federal government is attempting, through conferences like the one being held this week, with the help of the industry, to develop a safety net system to assist producers in managing risk better. At the same time, it is essential that these safety nets do not interfere with the way in which farmers make their management decisions, nor hamper Canada in marketing our agricultural products abroad.
I think it is important to mention briefly the four basic principles of the foundation of the agriculture policy review. First, national agricultural policies must be market responsive. Our agriculture industry must be
able to respond to market signals and demands, both in Canada and abroad. Opportunities for value-added production and diversification must be pursued.
Second, the industry must be self-reliant. This means federal policies and programs must nurture a climate of opportunity, without undermining the independence of the industry. Third, agriculture in this country must be sustainable. The long-term economic health of the industry depends to a large degree on a clean, healthy environment. Sustainable agricultural production must be economically viable.
Finally, a national agricultural strategy must be sensitive to the regional differences in this country. It must build on regional strengths and resources.
A vital part of the development of a national strategy for Canadian agriculture is consultation with the industry. The federal government is seeking input from farmers and from industry representatives from across Canada representing the many sectors of Canadian agriculture.
In closing, I would like to stress that we cannot look at stabilization of farm-fed grain in isolation from other agricultural policies and programs.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak in favour of the motion which is before the House today. I think that the views which have been expressed in this House have been to the point, particularly in respect of this bill. However, I think that there is a broader issue that must be discussed when looking at this issue and, in fact, when looking at other issues in respect of agriculture.
All agricultural programs must be discussed with some broader objectives in mind. We must ask ourselves the question, what future do we want for agriculture in this country. That is a question that in the past has not been addressed properly or with any real sincerity. The basic question with respect to agriculture is, of course, do we wish to maintain viable family farming units or do we wish to move to the industrial corporate farming model.
Since World War II, the programs and policies that have been implemented by various Liberal and Conservative governments through the years have not had any underlying foundation or any underlying base to them. Often we found programs and policies that have been divergent, that have not accomplished the tasks which
December 11, 1989

they set out to accomplish. It is important that we address our attention to this fundamental issue.
The government has put together a paper Growing Together, and there is a conference that is presently taking place. There are four pillars which have been suggested and which have been recounted by the government a number of times. Just to review them very briefly, they are calling for more market responsiveness, greater self-reliance, a national policy which recognizes diversity and increased environmental sustainability.
Those are very general concepts which can be supported in the abstract. The question, of course, is how will these translate into actual government policy. I think it is clear from attending the conference today that the direction this government is going in is a direction that is not considering the future viability of family farms. It is encouraging and moving toward the industrial corporate model and that is the direction that this government has chosen to take and I believe will be submitting policies with respect to that end.
This is a good opportunity to discuss agricultural issues but it is unfortunate that the government will be taking that direction. The government does state that it is a government of consultation. It is a government that desires to maintain a family farm model. But the evidence is not there. Certainly other bills that have recently been passed do not project that. Certainly the bill on advance payments which was recently passed increased the amount of advance payments to a limit of $250,000.1 do not know how many small producers, even medium producers, can take advantage of a $250,000 loan. That is a large amount of money. It is simply passing that legislation to the detriment of the family farmer in this country.
The idea of consultation that the government says it is entering into is certainly not clear from its handling of the oats issue. There was an outcry across this country when the government announced that it was going to remove oats from the Canadian Wheat Board. I and my colleagues have been in this House every day introducing petition after petition calling for the government to maintain oats under the Canadian Wheat Board. In fact, I just received today an answer to one of those petitions which says after careful consideration of the unique market potential for Canadian oats and in consideration of how that market could best be served, a decision was made to have the industry market oats. This change was

made solely in the best interests of the Canadian oats producer.
The Canadian oats producers do not want that. In fact, it is very clear that over two-thirds of producers in western Canada would prefer oats to remain under the Canadian Wheat Board. There is not consultation in the general sense of the word. There is simply consultation with those groups that agree with the government's position. That is unfortunate for the government. It is unfortunate for the producers and it is unfortunate for the people of this country.
There is also a broader issue that deals with rural Canada. We have to address the future of agriculture. We have to address the future of rural Canada generally. That includes small business, seniors and young people.
Across this country, many of the issues that are of concern to rural Saskatchewan are also the same concerns that exist in rural Nova Scotia, rural Prince Edward Island, rural Quebec or rural Ontario. The fact is that the rural infrastructure in this country is collapsing. Unless something is done to change that trend, rural Canada is in very severe trouble.
Certainly the small business people are closing their doors. Seniors are not remaining in communities where they grew up because of the lack of health care and transportation services and the lack of other amenities. Young families are not moving there for the same reason.
There needs to be a viable economic base in those communities in rural Canada in order to help maintain those areas. Certainly the recent projections for farm income reveal that fact. While farm income is projected to be down by 50 per cent across Canada, western Canada is severely hit. In the province of Saskatchewan, it is expected that people will have a negative net income next year, something that I find quite remarkable. Manitoba will be down by 87 per cent and Alberta by 54 per cent.
The producers in this country are in a severe financial situation. In my home province of Saskatchewan, we have something like over 39,000 farms which have an acreage of less than 1,000 acres and only 14,000 with acreages above 1,000 acres. The programs that are being developed and the way this government is talking is not looking at those smaller producers. Those producers, if they maintain themselves on the land, are the ones going into the general stores and buying the goods. They are the ones who are supporting the local pharmacies, doctors and dentists. If those people are gone, then there

Private Members' Business
is severe economic hardship for the community as a whole.
On this particular motion, I would like to make a couple of very short comments before my time runs out. The motion is really designed to help provide some equity and to help provide some fairness in the farming industry. If the goal is to encourage viable mixed farms in this country, then this motion should be supported by the government. We have the odd situation where a producer in times of low prices, instead of feeding the grain to his livestock which he would normally do, because of the situation is encouraged to deliver the grain to market. He is going to get a higher price for it because of the stabilization payment.
We have an irony here in that we have a free enterprise government which is hampering a farmer's ability to make some market decisions. What we want is to have some equity and some fairness in this program so that farmers can make those decisions and so that the farming economy will progress in a fashion that will be best for the local producers and allow them to make those decisions to maintain some viability.
We would ask that this bill be supported.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to say a few words about the Western Grain Stabilization Program and the Agricultural Stabilization Program.
All agriculture programs, including WGSA and ASA, are currently under review. The federal government has released a discussion paper to bring producers and their organizations into the policy review process. This paper is the focal point for discussion at the national agri-food policy conference being held at the Congress Centre today and tomorrow.
It is clear that our policies and programs need to change. We have worked with producers and their organizations to improve these programs in the past. The Western Grain Stabilization Program was amended in 1985 to improve the timing of issuing payments to producers. The act was amended so that producers would receive an interim payment in the spring during crop years when calculations indicated that there would be a substantial program payout. This amendment put cash in the hands of producers right before spring seeding when they needed it most.
In 1988 the Western Grain Stabilization Act was amended again.
